A wide base and a low centre of gravity mean the object must lean far before the critical line escapes; the tipping angle satisfies tan(angle) equal to half the base width divided by the centre of gravity height. A racing car with its mass 30 centimetres off the ground and a track 1.6 metres wide must tilt nearly 70 degrees to roll; a top-heavy SUV or a loaded furniture van reaches its limit far sooner, which is why rollover thresholds and static stability factors are regulated and published. The same reasoning explains the ubiquitous safety instructions of physical life. Load the heavy boxes low in the truck and the light ones high. Fill the bottom drawer of a filing cabinet first, and open only one drawer at a time, because an extended full drawer drags the combined centre of gravity forward toward the base's front edge; unanchored cabinets and toppling televisions injure thousands of children yearly, which is why furniture anchoring kits exist. A crane grows its base with outriggers before lifting; a fork-lift carries its load low and tilted back; a hiker leans uphill under a heavy pack. Your own body plays the game constantly: stand with heels and back against a wall and try to pick up a coin from the floor in front of you, and you will fail, because the wall prevents your hips from moving backward to keep the combined centre of gravity over your feet.

sections.heading: Couples: Pure Twist With No Net Push
sections.body: A couple is a pair of forces equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and offset so their lines of action do not coincide. Its net force is exactly zero, so it cannot accelerate an object's centre of mass anywhere; all it can do is rotate, which makes it the purest expression of torque in mechanics. The torque of a couple has a remarkable property: it is the same about every point in space, equal simply to F times d, one force's magnitude times the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action. The proof is a two-line calculation worth seeing. Take any pivot; one force acts at perpendicular distance x from it and the other at x plus d on the opposite side of its line, so the torques are minus F x and plus F times the quantity x plus d, summing to F d with every trace of x cancelled. Because the reference point drops out, a couple's torque is a free vector, and engineers speak of applying a pure moment to a shaft or joint without needing to say where. Human hands generate couples instinctively. Twisting a jar lid, you push forward with the fingers on one side and backward with the thumb on the other. Steering a car with hands at opposite sides of the wheel, one hand pushes up while the other pulls down; the wheel feels a pure twist and the steering column no net sideways load. Winding an old clock, turning a tap handle with two fingers, spinning a wing nut, wringing a towel: all couples. The wrench, by contrast, applies a single force at a distance, which delivers torque to the bolt but also a net sideways force that the bolt and your other hand must resist; a tap-and-die handle with two opposed arms exists precisely to convert that one-sided push into a balanced couple so the delicate tap cuts straight instead of bending. Couples are also the natural language of internal loading in structures. Cut a beam mentally at any cross-section and the material on one side exerts on the other both a force and an internal couple called the bending moment; it is this moment, not the shear force, that usually breaks beams, and bending-moment diagrams are the daily bread of structural engineering. The condition that a couple's torque never vanishes, no matter the pivot, restates a fact from equilibrium theory in sharper form: no single force, however placed, can balance a couple, because any single non-zero force violates force balance. Only another couple, equal and opposite in moment, can do it. That is why a helicopter with one main rotor cannot simply be flown straight: the engine torque spinning the rotor one way is a couple reacting on the fuselage the other way, and it must be cancelled by the tail rotor's thrust acting on a long lever arm, or by a second main rotor spinning opposite, as in tandem and coaxial designs.

sections.heading: Levers and Mechanical Advantage in Tools and the Body
sections.body: A lever is a rigid bar pivoting on a fulcrum, and it trades force against distance according to the torque balance: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. The ratio of the arms is the mechanical advantage. An advantage greater than one multiplies force at the cost of moving the effort end farther and faster than the load moves; an advantage less than one sacrifices force to gain speed and range. Since the work done, force times distance, balances on both sides in the frictionless ideal, a lever is not a source of energy, only an exchange rate. Tradition sorts levers into three classes by the arrangement of fulcrum, load, and effort. In a first-class lever the fulcrum sits between effort and load: seesaws, crowbars, pliers, scissors, and the oar of a rowing boat pivoting in its lock. In a second-class lever the load sits between fulcrum and effort, guaranteeing an advantage greater than one because the effort arm is necessarily longer: wheelbarrows, bottle openers, nutcrackers, and a door pushed at the handle against the resistance of its own hinges. In a third-class lever the effort acts between fulcrum and load, guaranteeing an advantage less than one but amplifying speed: tweezers, fishing rods, hockey sticks, tongs, and most of the human skeleton. The numbers make it vivid. A 1.5-metre crowbar with its fulcrum 5 centimetres from the load end gives a mechanical advantage of 145 divided by 5, about 29; a 300-newton human heave becomes nearly 9,000 newtons at the tip, enough to lift the edge of a small car, though the tip moves only one twenty-ninth as far as the hands. The human forearm runs the trade the other way. The biceps tendon inserts on the radius roughly 5 centimetres from the elbow's pivot, while a mass held in the hand sits about 35 centimetres out, a mechanical advantage of one-seventh. Holding a 10-kilogram dumbbell, roughly 98 newtons, therefore demands about 700 newtons of biceps tension, and the joint surfaces bear the difference in compression. Evolution accepted this apparent inefficiency because the payoff is speed: a small, fast muscle contraction near the joint sweeps the hand through a large, fast arc, which is what throwing, striking, and catching actually require. Standing on tiptoe is a second-class lever, ball of the foot as fulcrum, body weight rising between it and the calf muscles pulling up at the heel; the jaw is a first-and-third-class hybrid whose short arms let modest muscles crack nuts at the molars. Archimedes allegedly demonstrated compound leverage by hauling a loaded ship along the shore single-handed with a system of levers and pulleys. The lesson survives in every workshop: when a task needs more force, do not find a stronger person, find a longer arm, and when it needs more speed, shorten the arm and pay for it in effort.

sections.heading: Stable, Unstable, and Neutral: The Three Flavours of Equilibrium
sections.body: Zero net force and zero net torque describe a balance, but they say nothing about what happens when the balance is disturbed, and the difference is everything in practice. Displace an object slightly and watch the torques that appear. If they push the object back toward its original position, the equilibrium is stable: a marble at the bottom of a bowl, a pendulum hanging straight down, a rocking chair. If the disturbance awakens torques that drive the object farther away, the equilibrium is unstable: a marble balanced on top of an overturned bowl, a pencil standing on its point, a coin on edge. If displacement produces no restoring or amplifying torque at all, the equilibrium is neutral: a ball on a flat table, a wheel free on its axle. Gravity translates these cases into a single question about the centre of gravity. Any tilt of an object pivots it about an edge of its base of support, and the tilt momentarily raises or lowers the centre of gravity. If a small tilt raises the centre of gravity, gravity's torque opposes the tilt and the object is stable; if it lowers it, gravity assists the fall. Stable systems therefore sit at local minima of gravitational potential energy, unstable ones at maxima, and neutral ones on level plateaus, a principle that generalises far beyond gravity into chemistry, electronics, and economics. The depth of the minimum measures robustness. A pyramid on its base needs an enormous disturbance to reach its tipping edge; the same pyramid on its apex is in equilibrium too, mathematically, but the smallest breeze selects a direction of collapse. Engineers quantify this margin as the metacentric height in ships, the distance by which the effective pivot of a heeling hull sits above the centre of gravity; a positive metacentric height rights the vessel, while cargo loaded too high, or water sloshing on a vehicle deck, turns a stable ship unstable, the mechanism behind the 1987 Herald of Free Enterprise disaster and many capsizes since. Instability is not always the enemy; sometimes it is the mechanism. A light switch and a mousetrap are designed unstable in the middle so they snap decisively to one side. Standing humans operate an actively stabilised instability: the ankle joint sits below the body's centre of gravity, so upright posture is an inverted pendulum that would topple in about a second if the nervous system did not continuously sense sway and command small corrective ankle and hip torques; this is why standing still is tiring, why balance degrades when sensation or reaction time do, and why a walking robot is a control problem before it is a mechanical one. Between the extremes lie systems engineered to be just stable enough: a racing bicycle, twitchy but controllable; an airliner, strongly stable so it flies hands-off; a fighter jet, deliberately built near instability for agility and kept honest by computers making corrections dozens of times per second.

sections.heading: Where Analyses Fail: Common Errors and the Limits of Statics
sections.body: Torque problems fail in stereotyped ways, and knowing the catalogue is the fastest route to reliable answers. The most common error is a wrong lever arm: taking the full length of a strut, ladder, or beam when the torque needs only the perpendicular component, the length times the sine or cosine of the tilt angle. The cure is geometric, not algebraic: draw the line of action of each force, drop the perpendicular from the pivot, and label that distance before writing any equation. Second is the forgotten force, most often the object's own weight acting at its centre of gravity, or a reaction the problem's wording never mentions, like friction at a ladder's foot; the free-body diagram exists precisely to make forgetting visible. Third is the sign slip, one torque assigned clockwise when it is counterclockwise; the defence is to ask, for each force separately, which way it alone would spin the body, and then to verify the finished solution by computing the net torque about a point never used in the solving. Fourth is misplacing the pivot mid-problem, computing some lever arms from one point and some from another; all distances in a single torque equation must be measured from the same reference. Beyond the errors lie the genuine limits of the theory itself. Statics treats bodies as perfectly rigid, but nothing is; beams sag, bolts stretch, and floors flex. Usually the deformations are small enough to ignore, but statically indeterminate structures, a beam clamped at both ends, a table on four legs, cannot be solved at all without them, because they carry more unknown reactions than equilibrium supplies equations, and the material's stiffness decides the split. Statics also says nothing about strength: a bookshelf bracket can satisfy every equilibrium equation and still snap, because equilibrium constrains the loads, not the material's capacity to bear them; that is the province of stress analysis, and the reason a calculated reaction force must always be compared against a rated capacity with a safety factor, commonly 2 to 4 for structures and 5 or more for lifting gear. Real loading is rarely as gentle as the static picture: a jerked wrench, a jumped-on ladder rung, or a gust on a crane multiplies the instantaneous forces well beyond their static values, which is why dynamic or impact factors enter every serious design code, and why torque specifications for fasteners assume smooth, slow tightening. Friction introduces its own treachery, since static friction is an inequality, not an equation: it supplies whatever force equilibrium demands up to its limit and then lets go all at once, so a ladder or a braced shelf can stand for months and fail in an instant when a small extra load crosses the threshold. When an analysis matters, check it three ways: confirm the units of every term, test limiting cases where the answer is obvious, such as a load directly over a support, and recompute the torque balance about a fresh pivot. Agreement from independent directions is the closest statics comes to a guarantee.

guides.title: Kinematics: Describing Motion
guides.summary: How physics describes motion precisely: position, velocity and acceleration, the equations of constant acceleration, projectile and circular motion, relative frames, and the graphical and calculus tools that connect them, with worked numerical examples.

sections.heading: What Kinematics Is, and Why Description Comes Before Explanation
sections.body: Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes how things move without asking why they move. It deals in positions, times, velocities and accelerations, and it says nothing about forces, masses or energy. That deliberate silence is not a limitation but a strategy. Before Galileo, attempts to understand motion tangled description together with causal explanation, so that the question of how a thrown stone travels was inseparable from disputed claims about what kept it going after it left the hand. Aristotle's physics held that continued motion required a continued cause, which forced awkward theories in which the air closed behind the stone and pushed it forward. By separating the two questions, physics gained a description that could be measured and checked independently of any theory of causes, and that description turned out to be the foundation everything else was built on. Galileo Galilei made the decisive break in the early seventeenth century, and his method is worth noticing because it is the method of the whole subject. Free fall was too fast to time with the instruments of 1604, so he diluted gravity by rolling bronze balls down an inclined plane, timing them with a water clock that weighed the water escaping through a small tube. He found that the distance travelled grew as the square of the time: in successive equal intervals the ball covered distances in the ratio one, three, five, seven, and the total distances therefore went as one, four, nine, sixteen. That single quantitative result, published in the Discourses of 1638, is the origin of the kinematic equations still taught today, and it established that the natural description of falling is constant acceleration rather than constant speed. The subject rests on a small number of defined quantities and the relations among them. Position tells you where something is relative to an agreed origin; displacement is the change in position; velocity is the rate at which position changes; acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. Each is obtained from the previous one by differentiation with respect to time, and each is recovered from the next by integration. That chain, position to velocity to acceleration, and back again, is the entire logical content of kinematics, and every problem in the field is an application of it. The practical reach of the subject is enormous. Ballistics, vehicle stopping distances, orbital transfers, the timing of traffic lights, animation, robot arm control, machine tool paths and accident reconstruction are all kinematics problems. A police investigator measuring a skid mark to estimate a car's speed before braking, an engineer computing whether a lift will decelerate comfortably, and a navigator computing a course correction are all applying the same handful of relations. The rest of this treatment builds them carefully, because a mistake at the level of definition propagates into every later result.

sections.heading: Frames of Reference, Coordinates and the Meaning of Position
sections.body: No statement about motion means anything until a frame of reference has been chosen. A passenger seated in a train travelling at 120 kilometres per hour is simultaneously motionless with respect to the carriage, moving at 120 kilometres per hour with respect to the track, moving at roughly 460 metres per second eastward with respect to the Earth's axis if they are near the equator, and moving at about 30 kilometres per second with respect to the Sun. None of these descriptions is more correct than the others. A frame of reference is a choice of origin, a set of axes and a clock, and every position, velocity and acceleration is stated relative to that choice. To specify a position you need an origin, a set of directions, and units. In one dimension a single signed number suffices: a car at x equals minus 40 metres is 40 metres to the left of the chosen origin. In two or three dimensions position becomes a vector, conventionally written r, with components along the chosen axes, so that r equals x i plus y j plus z k, where i, j and k are unit vectors along the three axes. The SI unit of length is the metre, defined since 1983 as the distance light travels in vacuum in one 299,792,458th of a second, and the unit of time is the second, defined by 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the caesium-133 hyperfine transition. The distinction between distance and displacement is the first place students go wrong, and it matters. Displacement is the vector from the starting position to the ending position; distance is the total path length actually travelled. A runner completing one lap of a 400 metre track has a distance of 400 metres and a displacement of zero. A walker who goes 3 kilometres east then 4 kilometres north has travelled 7 kilometres but is displaced 5 kilometres from the start, by Pythagoras, at a bearing of about 37 degrees east of north. Displacement is a vector, carrying both magnitude and direction; distance is a scalar, a plain number with units. The same split runs through the whole subject: velocity is a vector and speed is its magnitude, so a car going round a roundabout at a steady 30 kilometres per hour has constant speed and continuously changing velocity. Coordinate systems other than the Cartesian one are often more convenient. Polar coordinates describe a position by a distance r from the origin and an angle theta, which makes circular motion trivial to write. Cylindrical and spherical coordinates extend this to three dimensions and are standard in problems with axial or central symmetry. The physics is identical in every system; only the algebra changes, and choosing well can turn a page of work into two lines.

sections.heading: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and the Idea of a Limit
sections.body: Average velocity is defined as displacement divided by the time interval over which it occurred: v average equals delta x over delta t. A car that is 90 kilometres further along a road after one hour has an average velocity of 90 kilometres per hour, or 25 metres per second, regardless of what happened in between. It may have stopped for fifteen minutes and then travelled at 120. Average velocity discards all detail of the journey and reports only the net effect, which is exactly what makes it useful for planning and useless for describing. Note that average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are different quantities, and the difference is not pedantry. A delivery van that drives 20 kilometres out and 20 kilometres back in two hours has an average speed of 20 kilometres per hour and an average velocity of exactly zero, because its displacement is zero. Another classic trap: if you drive one leg at 40 kilometres per hour and the return leg at 60, the average speed is not 50. Equal distances at different speeds take unequal times, so the correct figure is the harmonic mean, two times 40 times 60 divided by 100, which is 48 kilometres per hour. Time spent, not distance covered, is what averages weight. Instantaneous velocity is what a speedometer reports and what the physics of a moment requires. It is obtained by shrinking the measuring interval toward zero: v equals the limit as delta t approaches zero of delta x over delta t, which is precisely the derivative dx by dt. The conceptual difficulty here is genuine and was debated for two centuries. Motion over an interval of literally zero duration produces zero displacement in zero time, which is meaningless as a ratio; Bishop Berkeley mocked the early calculus for reasoning with ghosts of departed quantities. The resolution, formalised by Cauchy and Weierstrass in the nineteenth century, is that the derivative is not a ratio of two zeros but the limiting value the ratio approaches, which can be perfectly well defined even though no single interval realises it. A worked example makes it concrete. Suppose position in metres is given by x equals 2 t squared plus 3 t, with t in seconds. Between t equals 2 and t equals 3, the positions are 14 and 27 metres, so the average velocity is 13 metres per second. Shrink the interval to between 2 and 2.1 and the average becomes 11.2; between 2 and 2.01 it is 11.02. The values converge on 11, and indeed the derivative dx by dt equals 4 t plus 3, which at t equals 2 gives exactly 11 metres per second. That convergence is what instantaneous velocity means, and the same procedure underlies every speed measurement made by radar, by a wheel encoder, or by successive satellite fixes.

sections.heading: Acceleration: Changing Velocity, and Why It Is Not Just Speeding Up
sections.body: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time. Its average form is a equals delta v over delta t, and its instantaneous form is the derivative dv by dt, which is also the second derivative of position, d squared x by dt squared. The SI unit is metres per second per second, written as metres per second squared, and the unit is worth reading aloud in full because it says what the quantity is: a change of so many metres per second, in each second. A car accelerating at 3 metres per second squared gains 3 metres per second of velocity every second, reaching about 108 kilometres per hour in ten seconds if it starts from rest. The most persistent misconception in the whole subject is that acceleration means going faster. Acceleration is any change in velocity, and since velocity is a vector, it changes if the speed changes, if the direction changes, or if both change. A car braking has acceleration opposite to its motion, often called deceleration, though the physics is simply negative acceleration in the chosen positive direction. A satellite in a perfectly circular orbit travels at constant speed and is accelerating continuously, because its direction is always changing; the acceleration points toward the centre of the circle. A ball at the very top of its flight has zero velocity but is accelerating downward at the full 9.81 metres per second squared, which is why it does not remain there. The three quantities are logically independent: velocity can be zero while acceleration is large, and acceleration can be zero while velocity is large. Signs deserve care because they encode direction, not merit. If upward is chosen as positive, then gravity gives an acceleration of minus 9.81 metres per second squared for everything, rising or falling. A ball thrown upward has positive velocity and negative acceleration on the way up, meaning it is slowing, and negative velocity with the same negative acceleration on the way down, meaning it is speeding up. The rule that captures both cases is simple: when velocity and acceleration share a sign the object speeds up, and when they have opposite signs it slows down. Real accelerations span a wide range and it helps to have anchors. A comfortable lift accelerates at about 1 metre per second squared. A family car reaching 100 kilometres per hour in 10 seconds averages 2.8. Emergency braking on dry asphalt gives roughly 8 to 9, limited by the tyre friction coefficient of about 0.8 to 0.9. Fighter pilots tolerate around 9 g, roughly 88 metres per second squared, briefly and with a pressure suit. The rate of change of acceleration is itself a named quantity, jerk, measured in metres per second cubed, and controlling it is why well-designed lifts and trains ease into motion rather than snatching.

sections.heading: The Constant-Acceleration Equations and Where They Come From
sections.body: When acceleration is constant, four equations relate the five quantities of the problem: initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a, displacement s and time t. They are often called the suvat equations after those symbols. Each equation omits exactly one of the five, so the working technique is to identify which quantity you neither know nor want, and pick the equation that leaves it out. The first is v equals u plus a t, which omits displacement. It follows immediately from the definition of constant acceleration: if velocity changes by a every second, then after t seconds it has changed by a t. The second is s equals u t plus one half a t squared, which omits final velocity. It can be derived by noting that with constant acceleration the average velocity over the interval is simply the mean of the initial and final values, so s equals one half of u plus v, times t, and substituting v from the first equation. The third, s equals one half of u plus v times t, omits acceleration, and is the average-velocity statement itself. The fourth is v squared equals u squared plus 2 a s, which omits time and is obtained by eliminating t between the first two. It is the workhorse whenever a problem gives distances and speeds but no clock. There is a fifth, sometimes listed, s equals v t minus one half a t squared, which omits initial velocity and is useful when working backwards from a known final state. Every one of these can be read off a velocity-time graph without algebra: a straight line of slope a starting at height u gives v equals u plus a t directly, and the area under that line, a rectangle of area u t plus a triangle of area one half times t times a t, gives the displacement equation. The graphical derivation is worth learning because it survives when the algebra is forgotten. A worked case shows the machinery. A car travelling at 25 metres per second brakes at 7 metres per second squared. How far does it travel before stopping, and how long does it take? Time is not asked for and not given, so use the fourth equation with v equals 0, u equals 25 and a equals minus 7: 0 equals 625 minus 14 s, giving s equals 44.6 metres. For the time, the first equation gives 0 equals 25 minus 7 t, so t equals 3.6 seconds. Adding a reaction time of 1.5 seconds at 25 metres per second contributes 37.5 metres of thinking distance, so the total stopping distance is about 82 metres. Because braking distance depends on the square of speed, a driver at 35 metres per second needs 87.5 metres of braking rather than 44.6, nearly double for a 40 per cent speed increase. That square law is the single most important practical consequence of these four equations. It also explains why speed limits near schools are set so low.

sections.heading: Free Fall and the Measured Value of g
sections.body: Free fall is motion under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected. Its defining property, and the one that shocked contemporaries, is that the acceleration is the same for every object regardless of mass. A hammer and a feather released together in a vacuum land together, a result demonstrated theatrically by astronaut David Scott on the Moon in August 1971 during Apollo 15, where the absence of atmosphere made the vacuum condition real. On Earth the standard value of the acceleration due to gravity, symbol g, is 9.80665 metres per second squared by international definition, and 9.81 is accurate enough for almost all work. The true local value varies: about 9.78 at the equator, where the Earth's rotation and equatorial bulge both reduce it, and about 9.83 at the poles, a spread of roughly half a per cent. It falls with altitude by approximately 3 parts in ten million per metre of ascent. Applying the constant-acceleration equations to free fall is straightforward once a sign convention is fixed. Taking downward as positive and dropping an object from rest, the distance fallen is one half g t squared, so after 1 second it has fallen 4.9 metres, after 2 seconds 19.6 metres, and after 3 seconds 44.1 metres, reproducing Galileo's squares. Speed after a fall of height h is the square root of 2 g h, which gives a memorable rule: falling 5 metres, roughly a first-floor window, produces an impact speed near 10 metres per second, or 36 kilometres per hour. Falling from 20 metres doubles that to about 20 metres per second. Because impact energy scales with the square of speed, and therefore linearly with height, fall injury severity rises sharply with height, with survival becoming unlikely above roughly 12 to 15 metres for an unprotected adult onto a hard surface, though outcomes vary enormously with landing surface and posture. Air resistance eventually breaks the idealisation, and it does so in a specific way. Drag force grows roughly with the square of speed for objects moving fast enough through air, so as a falling body accelerates the drag rises until it balances the weight, after which the net acceleration is zero and the speed stops increasing. That equilibrium speed is terminal velocity. A skydiver in a spread-eagled belly-to-earth position reaches roughly 55 metres per second, about 200 kilometres per hour, after about 12 seconds and 450 metres of fall; head-down in a tracking position the same person may exceed 90 metres per second. A raindrop 2 millimetres across terminates near 6 metres per second, a mist droplet at a few centimetres per second, which is why fog appears to hang. Kinematics with constant acceleration describes free fall accurately only until drag becomes comparable to weight, which for a compact dense object is a matter of several seconds and for a sheet of paper is almost immediate.

sections.heading: Reading Motion Graphs: Slopes, Areas and Curvature
sections.body: Graphs are not a teaching aid bolted onto kinematics; they are the most direct representation of what the quantities mean, and a great many problems that look formidable in algebra become obvious when drawn. Three graph types recur: position against time, velocity against time, and acceleration against time. Two operations connect them. The slope of a graph gives the derivative, so the slope of a position-time graph at any instant is the instantaneous velocity, and the slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration. The area between a graph and the time axis gives the integral, so the area under a velocity-time curve is the displacement, and the area under an acceleration-time curve is the change in velocity. Area below the axis counts as negative. On a position-time graph, a horizontal line means the object is at rest, a straight sloped line means constant velocity, and a curve means acceleration. Curvature that opens upward corresponds to positive acceleration and curvature opening downward to negative. A ball thrown straight up traces a downward-opening parabola on this graph, and the peak of the parabola is the highest point of the flight, where the slope, and therefore the velocity, is momentarily zero. A crossing of the horizontal axis means passing the origin, not stopping, which is a common misreading. On a velocity-time graph, the horizontal line means constant velocity, a sloped line means constant acceleration, and the sign of the value, not the slope, tells you which way the object is moving. A line crossing the time axis marks a reversal of direction, and this is the moment where displacement stops growing and starts shrinking. To find total distance rather than displacement from such a graph, you must add the magnitudes of the areas above and below the axis separately rather than letting them cancel. A vehicle that accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds covers the area of a triangle, one half times 10 times 20, which is 100 metres, a result you can read off in seconds without touching an equation. Two habits make graph reading reliable. First, always identify what is plotted before interpreting anything, because a position-time graph and a velocity-time graph of the same journey look completely different and confusing them is the single most common examination error. Second, check the endpoints and the sign changes rather than the middle, since these carry the physical events: the moment of maximum height, the instant of reversal, the point where acceleration ceases. Real instrumentation, such as accident data recorders in vehicles or accelerometer traces from a phone, produces exactly these graphs, and the same slope-and-area reading extracts the story from them. A crash investigator reading a five-second velocity trace can identify the instant the driver lifted off the accelerator, the onset of braking, and the impact, purely from changes of slope.

sections.heading: Vectors, and Why Motion in a Plane Splits Into Independent Parts
sections.body: Motion in two or three dimensions requires vectors, and the single most powerful idea in this part of the subject is that the components of a vector along perpendicular axes behave independently. A vector has magnitude and direction and can be written either in that polar form or as components: a velocity of 20 metres per second at 30 degrees above the horizontal has a horizontal component of 20 times the cosine of 30, which is 17.3 metres per second, and a vertical component of 20 times the sine of 30, which is 10.0 metres per second. Going the other way, components of 3 and 4 give a magnitude of 5 by Pythagoras and a direction given by the arctangent of 4 over 3, about 53 degrees. Vectors add tip to tail, which is equivalent to adding their components separately, and this componentwise rule is what makes the whole approach work. The independence of perpendicular components is a physical claim, not merely an algebraic convenience, and Galileo was the first to state it clearly. If a cannonball is fired horizontally from a cliff at the same instant an identical ball is simply dropped, both strike the ground at the same moment. Horizontal motion does not affect vertical fall, and vertical fall does not affect horizontal travel. The demonstration is easy to reproduce with a coin flicked off a table edge beside a coin pushed straight off: the two clicks arrive together. What makes this true is that gravity acts vertically and therefore has no horizontal component to change the horizontal velocity. Consequently a two-dimensional problem is solved by decomposing it into two one-dimensional problems that share only one thing, the clock. Time is the common variable that stitches the components back together, which is why the standard technique is to solve whichever component gives you the time and then feed that time into the other. In three dimensions the same applies with a third axis. Position, velocity and acceleration are all vectors, related component by component: the x-component of velocity is the derivative of the x-component of position, and so on. Two vector operations appear constantly. The scalar or dot product of two vectors, a dot b, equals the product of their magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between them, and it yields a plain number; it is how you extract the component of one vector along another, and how you test for perpendicularity, since perpendicular vectors have zero dot product. The vector or cross product, a cross b, has magnitude equal to the product of the magnitudes times the sine of the included angle and points perpendicular to both by the right-hand rule; it appears in rotational kinematics, where the velocity of a point on a rotating body equals the angular velocity vector crossed with the position vector. Choosing axes wisely is a real skill. On an inclined plane, taking the axes along and perpendicular to the slope rather than horizontal and vertical reduces the algebra substantially, because then the motion is entirely along one axis.

sections.heading: Projectile Motion: The Parabola and Its Consequences
sections.body: A projectile is any object moving under gravity alone after an initial launch, with air resistance neglected. Its treatment is the classic application of component independence: the horizontal acceleration is zero, so horizontal velocity is constant, while the vertical acceleration is a constant g downward. Writing the launch speed as u at an angle theta above the horizontal, the horizontal position is x equals u cos theta times t, and the vertical position is y equals u sin theta times t minus one half g t squared. Eliminating t between them gives y as a quadratic function of x, which is the equation of a parabola. That the trajectory is a parabola was Galileo's discovery and it follows entirely from the constancy of g. Several standard results follow. The time to reach maximum height is u sin theta divided by g, because the vertical velocity component must fall to zero. The maximum height itself is u squared times sine squared theta, divided by 2 g. For launch and landing at the same height, the total flight time is twice the rise time, and the horizontal range is u squared times the sine of twice theta, divided by g. That last formula carries the well-known consequence that the range is greatest at 45 degrees, since the sine of 90 degrees is its maximum of one, and that pairs of angles adding to 90 degrees give equal ranges: 30 and 60 degrees both send a projectile the same distance, though by very different paths and flight times. A worked example fixes the method. A ball is kicked at 20 metres per second at 40 degrees. The components are 15.3 horizontally and 12.9 vertically. Rise time is 12.9 divided by 9.81, which is 1.31 seconds, so the total flight is 2.62 seconds and the maximum height is 8.4 metres. Range is 15.3 times 2.62, giving 40.1 metres, which matches the range formula. If instead the ball is kicked from a 10 metre cliff, the landing is no longer symmetric and you must solve the vertical quadratic for when y equals minus 10, taking the positive root, then multiply by the horizontal velocity. The neglect of air resistance is not a small approximation for real projectiles. A struck baseball that would travel 180 metres in vacuum travels about 120 metres in air. Drag both shortens the range and makes the trajectory asymmetric, with a steeper descent than ascent. The optimal launch angle drops below 45 degrees, typically to around 40 degrees for a thrown ball and to near 30 for a shot put, and to far lower angles for high-velocity bullets, where the ballistic coefficient governs everything. Spin adds lift or curve through the Magnus effect, which is why a golf ball with backspin flies much further than the vacuum parabola predicts and why a curveball bends. Kinematics gives the skeleton; real ballistics adds a drag model on top of it.

sections.heading: Circular Motion and Centripetal Acceleration
sections.body: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating at every instant, because its direction of travel changes continuously. This acceleration is called centripetal, meaning centre-seeking, and it points directly toward the centre of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity at every moment. Its magnitude is v squared divided by r, where v is the speed and r the radius. The result can be derived geometrically: over a small time interval the velocity vector rotates through the same small angle as the position vector, so the change in velocity has magnitude v times the angle, and dividing by the time gives v times the angular rate, which equals v squared over r. The formula's structure is worth absorbing. Because speed enters squared, doubling the speed around the same bend quadruples the acceleration required, which is why cornering speed is so unforgiving. Because radius enters in the denominator, a tighter bend at the same speed demands more. A car taking a 50 metre radius bend at 15 metres per second requires 4.5 metres per second squared, comfortably within the roughly 8 metres per second squared that dry tyres can supply; at 25 metres per second the same bend demands 12.5, beyond the available grip, and the car leaves the road. This single calculation underlies road design, and it is why highway curves are given large radii and banked, since banking lets part of the road's normal reaction supply the centre-seeking direction. When speed also changes, the total acceleration has two perpendicular parts: the centripetal component v squared over r toward the centre, and a tangential component equal to the rate of change of speed, along the direction of travel. The magnitudes combine by Pythagoras. A car accelerating out of a bend experiences both simultaneously, and the vector sum is what the tyres must supply, which is the physical content of the friction circle used by racing drivers: you may spend your available grip on turning or on accelerating, but the total cannot exceed the limit. Two persistent misconceptions deserve correction. There is no outward force pushing a rotating object away from the centre in an inertial frame; the sensation of being flung outward in a turning car is the seat pushing you inward while your body tends to continue straight, and the so-called centrifugal force is a bookkeeping term that appears only when you insist on doing physics in the rotating frame itself. Second, centripetal acceleration is not a new kind of force but a requirement: some real force, friction, tension, gravity or a normal reaction, must supply it, and when none is available the object simply travels in a straight line, which is what a skidding car does. Orbits are the same relation with gravity supplying the acceleration; the International Space Station orbits at about 7.66 kilometres per second at a radius of roughly 6,780 kilometres.

sections.heading: Rotational Kinematics: Angles, Angular Velocity and Angular Acceleration
sections.body: When a rigid body rotates, every point on it sweeps a different distance but turns through the same angle, which makes angle the natural variable. Angular position theta is measured in radians, defined as the arc length divided by the radius, so that one full turn is 2 pi radians, approximately 6.283, and one radian is about 57.3 degrees. The radian is dimensionless by construction, which is why it can appear and disappear from formulas without upsetting the units, and it is the only angular measure in which the tidy relations below hold without conversion factors. Angular velocity omega is the rate of change of angle, d theta by dt, measured in radians per second, and angular acceleration alpha is d omega by dt, in radians per second squared. The entire structure of linear kinematics repeats exactly: for constant angular acceleration, omega equals omega naught plus alpha t, theta equals omega naught t plus one half alpha t squared, and omega squared equals omega naught squared plus 2 alpha theta. Anyone who has learned the linear equations already knows the rotational ones, with the substitutions of theta for s, omega for v and alpha for a. The bridge between rotational and linear descriptions is the radius. A point at distance r from the axis has tangential speed v equals omega r, tangential acceleration a equals alpha r, and centripetal acceleration omega squared r. This is why the rim of a grinding wheel is dangerous while its hub is not, and why a 30 centimetre disc spinning at 3,000 revolutions per minute has a rim speed of about 47 metres per second. To convert revolutions per minute into radians per second, multiply by 2 pi and divide by 60, so 3,000 revolutions per minute is 314 radians per second. Angular quantities are vectors, though in a slightly unfamiliar way. The direction of the angular velocity vector is taken along the axis of rotation, with the sense given by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of rotation and the thumb points along omega. This convention is what allows rotations to be handled with vector algebra, and it makes the relation v equals omega cross r exact. One genuine subtlety is that finite rotations do not commute and therefore are not vectors at all: rotating a book 90 degrees about one axis and then another gives a different final orientation than the reverse order, as anyone can verify with a book. Infinitesimal rotations, and hence angular velocities, do commute and are proper vectors. A worked example: a flywheel spinning at 120 radians per second is braked uniformly to rest in 40 seconds. The angular acceleration is minus 3 radians per second squared, and the total angle turned is one half times 120 times 40, which is 2,400 radians, or about 382 revolutions. If the wheel has a radius of 0.4 metres, a point on its rim starts at 48 metres per second and travels 960 metres of arc before stopping. Every quantity there came from the linear equations with different letters.

sections.heading: Relative Motion and the Galilean Transformation
sections.body: Because all motion is described relative to a frame, converting between frames is a routine and essential operation. The rule for velocities in classical physics is simple vector addition. If frame B moves with velocity v of B relative to frame A, and an object moves with velocity v of the object relative to B, then its velocity relative to A is the vector sum of the two. Written with the subscript convention that reads velocity of P relative to A equals velocity of P relative to B plus velocity of B relative to A, the inner subscripts cancel like fractions, which makes it easy to check. Reversing a subscript pair reverses the vector's sign. One-dimensional cases are intuitive. A passenger walking forward at 1.5 metres per second in a train moving at 30 metres per second travels at 31.5 metres per second relative to the ground; walking toward the rear, at 28.5. Two cars approaching each other at 25 and 20 metres per second close at 45 metres per second, which is why head-on collisions are so severe. Two-dimensional cases are where the technique earns its keep. An aircraft with an airspeed of 200 kilometres per hour heading due north in a crosswind of 50 kilometres per hour from the west has a ground velocity that is the vector sum: it moves at about 206 kilometres per hour on a track roughly 14 degrees east of north. To actually fly due north the pilot must crab into the wind, heading about 14.5 degrees west of north, and the resulting groundspeed drops to about 194. The same arithmetic applies to a swimmer crossing a river, and it explains the counterintuitive fact that in a river with uniform flow, aiming straight across gives the shortest crossing time even though it does not give the shortest path. An important structural fact is that acceleration is unchanged between frames moving at constant velocity relative to one another. Differentiating the velocity addition rule, the constant relative velocity differentiates to zero, so both observers measure the same acceleration. Frames related in this way are called inertial, and the transformation between them, in which x prime equals x minus V t while t prime equals t, is the Galilean transformation. This invariance is why you can pour a drink normally on a smooth cruising aircraft: nothing in the mechanics distinguishes uniform motion from rest. Accelerating frames are different, and in them apparent forces appear, such as the pseudo-force that pushes you back into your seat during takeoff and the Coriolis effect in the rotating frame of the Earth. The Galilean rule fails at speeds approaching that of light, where velocities combine by the relativistic formula and light itself is measured at 299,792,458 metres per second by every observer. The correction is negligible below about one per cent of light speed, so for all terrestrial engineering the classical addition rule is exact for practical purposes.

sections.heading: When Acceleration Varies: The Calculus of Motion
sections.body: The constant-acceleration equations are a special case, and applying them where acceleration is not constant is the most damaging error in the subject because it produces plausible wrong numbers rather than obvious nonsense. Real accelerations are usually not constant: a rocket's acceleration rises as it burns fuel and grows lighter, a car's acceleration falls as it changes up through the gears and as drag builds, a falling body's acceleration decreases toward zero as it approaches terminal velocity, and a mass on a spring has an acceleration proportional to its displacement. In all such cases the general calculus relations remain valid and the shortcut formulas do not. The general relations are compact. Velocity is the integral of acceleration with respect to time, and position is the integral of velocity, with each integration introducing a constant fixed by the initial conditions. Going the other way, velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration the derivative of velocity. If acceleration is given as a function of time, integrate. If it is given as a function of position rather than time, which happens with springs and with gravity at large distances, use the chain-rule identity a equals v times dv by dx, which converts the problem into one that can be separated and integrated in x. That identity is worth memorising because it unlocks an entire class of problems the suvat equations cannot touch. A worked example: suppose acceleration is a equals 6 t, starting from rest at the origin. Then velocity is the integral, 3 t squared, and position is t cubed. At t equals 4 seconds the velocity is 48 metres per second and the position 64 metres. Compare what the constant-acceleration formula would have given had someone naively used the final acceleration of 24 metres per second squared: a displacement of one half times 24 times 16, which is 192 metres, three times too large. The error is not subtle, and it is entirely a consequence of applying a formula outside its stated condition. Simple harmonic motion is the most important non-constant case. When acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed back toward the origin, a equals minus omega squared x, the solution is sinusoidal: x equals A cosine of omega t plus a phase, with velocity and acceleration also sinusoidal and shifted by a quarter and a half cycle respectively. The maximum speed is omega times the amplitude A and the maximum acceleration is omega squared times A. A pendulum of length L swings with omega equal to the square root of g over L for small angles, giving a period of 2 pi times the square root of L over g, which is about 2.0 seconds for a one metre pendulum. Where no closed-form solution exists, numerical integration by small time steps, the Euler or Runge-Kutta methods, is the standard approach and is what every physics simulation actually does.

sections.heading: A Reliable Method for Solving Kinematics Problems
sections.body: Most errors in kinematics are not conceptual but procedural: a sign dropped, a formula used outside its conditions, an angle measured from the wrong axis, units mixed between kilometres per hour and metres per second. A disciplined routine removes nearly all of them, and the routine below is the one used by physicists, engineers and accident investigators alike. It is worth following even on problems that look easy, because the habit is what saves you on the ones that are not. The single most valuable step is the first: draw the situation and commit to a coordinate system in writing. Nearly every sign error traces back to a positive direction that was never explicitly chosen or that silently changed halfway through the working. The second most valuable is the last: check the answer against physical sense before accepting it. A stopping distance of 4 kilometres, a projectile that lands before it was launched, or a speed exceeding that of light all indicate an error somewhere earlier, and noticing them costs seconds while submitting them costs everything.
steps: Draw a clear sketch of the motion, marking the start, the end, and any intermediate events such as the moment brakes are applied. Divide the motion into phases wherever the acceleration changes, and treat each phase as a separate problem linked by shared values at the boundary.

Choose an origin and a positive direction, and write them down. For vertical motion state whether up or down is positive; for two dimensions state both axes. Every subsequent sign follows from this choice and from nothing else.

Convert every quantity to consistent SI units before calculating. Divide kilometres per hour by 3.6 to get metres per second, and multiply revolutions per minute by 2 pi over 60 for radians per second. Mixed units are the most frequent source of order-of-magnitude errors.

List the five quantities for each phase: initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, displacement and time. Mark which are known, which is wanted, and which is neither. Watch for implicit values: starts from rest means the initial velocity is zero, and at the highest point of a projectile the vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal component is unchanged.
Confirm that acceleration is constant over the phase before using the suvat equations. If it varies with time or position, integrate instead.

For two-dimensional problems, resolve into perpendicular components and solve each as a separate one-dimensional problem. Solve whichever component determines the duration first, then use that time in the other component. Time is the only quantity the two components share.

Select the equation that omits the quantity you neither know nor want, then substitute with signs attached before doing any arithmetic. Keep symbols as long as possible and put numbers in at the end, which makes errors easier to trace and lets you check the units of the final expression.

Check the answer three ways: are the units correct, is the magnitude physically plausible, and does the sign point the direction you expect? Where possible, verify by a second route, such as recomputing a displacement from the area under a velocity-time graph.

sections.heading: Measuring Motion in Practice: Instruments and Uncertainty
sections.body: Kinematic quantities are measured, not merely calculated, and every real measurement carries uncertainty that propagates into whatever is derived from it. The oldest technique is timing over a known distance, which is what Galileo did with his water clock and what a stopwatch and a marked track still do. Its accuracy is limited by human reaction time, typically 0.2 to 0.3 seconds, which over a one-second interval is a 25 per cent error and over a ten-second interval a 2.5 per cent one. This is why school laboratories use light gates, which trigger electronically as an object interrupts a beam and resolve to a millisecond or better. Doppler radar and lidar measure velocity directly rather than inferring it. Radar transmits a microwave signal and measures the frequency shift of the return, which is proportional to the component of the target's velocity along the beam. That last qualification produces the cosine error: a device aimed at an angle to the direction of travel reads low by the cosine of that angle, which is why traffic enforcement devices are aimed nearly along the road. Lidar times the round trip of laser pulses and differentiates successive ranges. Satellite navigation systems derive both position and velocity, position from the timing of signals from at least four satellites and velocity more accurately from the Doppler shift of their carriers, giving typical position accuracy of a few metres and velocity accuracy of a few centimetres per second. Inertial measurement units, now in every smartphone, contain micro-machined accelerometers and gyroscopes. An accelerometer measures proper acceleration, which is the acceleration relative to free fall, so a device resting on a table reads 9.81 metres per second squared upward rather than zero, and a device in free fall reads zero. Extracting position requires integrating twice, and any constant bias in the sensor grows as one half b t squared, so a bias of just 0.01 metres per second squared produces a 180 metre position error after one minute. This integration drift is why inertial navigation is always corrected by an external reference such as satellite fixes or a wheel odometer, and why phone dead reckoning is unusable beyond a few seconds without help. Uncertainty propagates by known rules. For a velocity computed as distance over time, the fractional uncertainties add in quadrature, so a distance known to 1 per cent and a time known to 2 per cent give a velocity uncertain by about 2.2 per cent. For quantities that are squared, such as the v squared in a braking calculation, the fractional uncertainty doubles. High-speed video at 1,000 frames per second, common in sports and crash analysis, resolves events to a millisecond, but the accuracy of derived speed depends equally on the calibration of the distance scale in frame.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and the Limits of Kinematic Description
sections.body: Kinematics fails in predictable ways, and knowing them is as valuable as knowing the equations. The most common failure is applying the constant-acceleration formulas where acceleration is not constant. This is silent: the algebra works, the units come out right, and the answer is simply wrong, often by a factor of two or three. Any problem involving air resistance over more than a few seconds, a vehicle across a gear change, a spring, a rocket burn, or gravity over distances comparable to a planetary radius requires integration rather than the shortcut. The diagnostic question is always whether the acceleration is the same at the end of the interval as at the start. The second failure is sign and frame confusion, which produces answers of the right magnitude pointing the wrong way. Vertical problems with a chosen positive direction that flips halfway through, angles measured from the vertical when the formula expects them from the horizontal, and relative velocities with reversed subscripts are the usual culprits. The third is confusing scalars and vectors, most often by averaging speeds arithmetically over equal distances rather than weighting by time, or by reporting displacement when distance was wanted. A subtler class of failure concerns the idealisations themselves. Point-particle kinematics ignores the size and orientation of real objects, which matters for a tumbling projectile, for a long vehicle turning, and for anything where rotation and translation interact. The rigid-body assumption ignores deformation, which is precisely what absorbs energy in a crash and what makes a real bounce imperfect. Air, water and friction are outside kinematics entirely and must be brought in through dynamics. And any prediction extrapolated far beyond the measured interval compounds small errors: a velocity uncertain by 1 per cent gives a position uncertain by 1 per cent of the distance, which is metres over kilometres and kilometres over interplanetary distances. There are also hard physical limits. The Galilean picture, in which time is universal and velocities simply add, is an approximation that breaks down as speeds approach that of light. At 10 per cent of light speed the relativistic correction is about half a per cent; at 87 per cent it is a factor of two. Global positioning satellites must correct for both special and general relativistic effects, amounting to about 38 microseconds per day, or roughly 11 kilometres of position error if ignored. At the other extreme, quantum mechanics denies that a particle has a simultaneously definite position and momentum at all, with the uncertainty principle setting the product of the uncertainties at no less than about 1.055 times ten to the minus 34 joule seconds divided by two. For everything of ordinary size and speed, however, classical kinematics is accurate to far better than any measurement you are likely to make, and when a kinematic answer disagrees with reality the cause is almost always an unmodelled force, a wrong assumption about constancy, or a measurement error, not a failure of the framework.

guides.title: Projectile Motion and Trajectories
guides.summary: How objects move once they have been launched and left to gravity: the independence of horizontal and vertical motion, the parabola and its equations, and how air resistance, spin and the Earth's rotation bend real trajectories away from the textbook curve.

sections.heading: What Counts as a Projectile, and Why the Problem Matters
sections.body: A projectile is any object that has been given an initial push and is thereafter left to gravity and to whatever the surrounding air chooses to do to it. A thrown stone, a struck golf ball, a mortar bomb, a jet of water leaving a hose, a long jumper in mid flight, and a spacecraft coasting between engine burns are all projectiles in this technical sense. What unites them is the absence of thrust along the path. The launch is finished, the hand or the barrel or the club face has done its work, and from that instant the object is simply falling while it travels sideways. The moment a rocket motor is still burning, or a bird is still flapping, the object is not a projectile and the analysis below does not apply to it. This is the first problem in elementary mechanics in which two motions must be tracked at once, and that is precisely why it appears early in every physics course. Free fall along a single line is one dimensional bookkeeping. Circular motion demands reasoning about a direction that changes continuously. Projectile motion sits exactly between the two, and it can be solved completely by one insight: motion along the horizontal axis can be described entirely independently of motion along the vertical axis. Once a student genuinely believes that, a very large class of problems collapses into arithmetic. The practical stakes are considerable. Gunnery tables, the range settings on a mortar sight, the elevation of a fire hose nozzle, the trajectory of a basketball, the landing footprint of an aircraft dropping supplies, the design of a ski jump landing slope, and the flight of an irrigation sprinkler all rest on this analysis. Forensic reconstruction of a vehicle leaving a road, or of blood spatter, uses the same equations run backwards from a landing point to an initial speed. Civil engineers use them to size a spillway plunge pool. Sports coaches use them, usually without the algebra, to reason about release angles. It helps to see the subject as a ladder of models rather than a single formula. The bottom rung is the vacuum parabola: constant downward acceleration, nothing else. The next rung adds air resistance, which for anything moving faster than a gentle toss is not a small correction but often the dominant term. Above that sits spin, which makes a ball curve sideways or hang in the air. At the top, for shots measured in kilometres, sit the rotation of the Earth and the variation of air density with altitude. Each rung is a genuine improvement on the one below and each costs more mathematics. A competent practitioner knows which rung the problem in front of them actually requires, and does not solve a tennis serve with Coriolis terms or an artillery problem with a bare parabola.

sections.heading: Galileo and the Discovery of Compound Motion
sections.body: Before the seventeenth century the dominant account of thrown objects came from Aristotle and his medieval commentators. In that picture a projectile was pushed along by the air closing in behind it, travelled in a straight slanting line while its violent motion lasted, then at some point exhausted that impetus and fell more or less straight down. Illustrations in fifteenth century gunnery manuals show exactly this: a straight rising line, a short curved shoulder, and a near vertical plunge. The picture was not stupid. It matches what a cannonball actually seems to do when heavy air drag is present, and it was good enough that gunners built usable range tables on top of it. Galileo Galilei broke the problem apart. Working through the 1590s and publishing the mature argument in the Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Relating to Two New Sciences of 1638, he separated the horizontal from the vertical and treated each with its own law. Horizontally, in the absence of resistance, an object continues at whatever speed it was given, because nothing acts to change it. That claim is a statement of inertia, and it was the harder half of the insight, because everyday experience of friction and drag suggests the opposite. Vertically, the object accelerates downward uniformly, gaining equal increments of speed in equal times. Combining a uniform motion with a uniformly accelerated one at right angles produces, Galileo showed geometrically, a parabola. He had reached the uniform acceleration result by an ingenious experimental dodge. Free fall was too fast to time with the water clocks and pulse counting available to him, so he rolled bronze balls down grooved inclined planes, diluting gravity by a known geometric factor while leaving its character intact. The distances covered in successive equal time intervals stood in the ratio one, three, five, seven, which is exactly the signature of distance growing as the square of elapsed time. Whether he also performed the famous leaning tower demonstration is doubtful and probably legendary, but the inclined plane work is documented in his own notebooks. The synthesis was completed by Isaac Newton in the Principia of 1687, where the parabola becomes a corollary of a general law of motion plus a universal gravitational force, and where Newton adds the thought experiment that turns the subject inside out. Imagine a cannon on a very high mountain firing horizontally with ever greater speed. Each shot travels further before striking the ground. At a sufficient speed the curvature of the fall matches the curvature of the Earth and the ball never lands. It is in orbit. Orbital motion and a tossed apple are then the same phenomenon at different speeds, and the parabola is revealed as a close approximation to a very eccentric ellipse, valid whenever the range is small compared with the radius of the planet.

sections.heading: The Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
sections.body: The single load bearing idea in the whole subject is that the two components of the motion do not talk to each other. Gravity pulls straight down, so it changes only the vertical velocity. Nothing acts horizontally in the idealised case, so the horizontal velocity is whatever it was at launch and stays that way forever. The consequence is startling when first met: a bullet fired perfectly horizontally from a rifle and a bullet simply dropped from the muzzle at the same instant reach level ground at the same moment. One has travelled several hundred metres and the other has travelled none, but both have fallen the same distance in the same time. This is not a rhetorical trick, it is an experimental fact, and it is worth demonstrating rather than merely asserting. The classic apparatus is the monkey and hunter demonstration. A target is suspended from an electromagnet, and a projectile is aimed directly at it and fired. The act of firing cuts the current, so the target begins to fall at the instant the projectile leaves the launcher. The projectile hits the target every time, at any launch speed. The reason is that both objects accumulate exactly the same downward displacement, one half g t squared, in the same elapsed time, so the projectile's shortfall below its aiming line always equals the target's drop. A cheaper version uses a spring loaded device that simultaneously flicks one coin horizontally off a table and drops another; the two strike the floor with a single audible click. Formally, the independence follows because the acceleration vector has no horizontal component. Writing the position as two separate functions of the same clock, the horizontal coordinate is x equals v times the cosine of the launch angle times t, and the vertical is y equals v times the sine of the launch angle times t minus one half g t squared, where v is the launch speed, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and t is the time since launch. Time is the shared parameter that stitches the two together. Every projectile question is answered by finding the relevant time from one equation and substituting it into the other. The independence is exact only when the sole force is gravity. Air resistance destroys it, because drag acts along the direction of travel and therefore has both a horizontal and a vertical component that each depend on the total speed. That is why a real bullet does not quite obey the demonstration, and why strong crosswinds cannot be handled by simply adding a sideways correction to a vertical solution. The independence is a property of the vacuum model, not a universal truth, and understanding where it comes from is what tells you when it is safe to lean on it.

sections.heading: The Kinematic Equations and How to Set Up a Problem
sections.body: The full description of ideal projectile motion needs four equations and one shared clock. Choose axes first, because half of all errors are sign errors. The usual convention takes the launch point as the origin, x positive in the direction of travel, y positive upward, and therefore the acceleration equal to minus g, where g is approximately 9.81 metres per second squared at the Earth's surface. That value is not a constant of nature. It varies from about 9.780 at the equator to 9.832 at the poles, because the Earth bulges and rotates, and it falls by roughly 0.003 per thousand metres of altitude. For most work 9.81 is ample; for precision gunnery the local value matters. Resolve the launch velocity into components once, at the start. If the projectile leaves at speed v and angle theta above the horizontal, the horizontal component is v cos theta and the vertical component is v sin theta. The horizontal velocity then never changes. The vertical velocity at time t is v sin theta minus g t, which passes through zero at the top of the arc and becomes increasingly negative on the way down. Position follows by integration: x equals v cos theta times t, and y equals v sin theta times t minus one half g t squared. A fourth relation, obtained by eliminating time, gives the vertical velocity in terms of height alone: the square of the vertical velocity equals the square of its launch value minus two g times the height gained. That form is useful whenever a problem specifies heights but not times. A reliable procedure is to list what is known in each column, horizontal and vertical, before writing anything else. The horizontal column holds a constant velocity and possibly a distance. The vertical column holds the initial vertical velocity, the acceleration, and either a height or a final vertical velocity. Whichever column is fully determined yields the time of flight, which is then handed to the other. If neither is complete, the missing piece is usually a geometric constraint such as landing on a slope or clearing a wall of stated height. Two subtleties trip people repeatedly. First, the projectile passes through most heights twice, once rising and once falling, so solving a quadratic for time will legitimately give two positive roots and you must decide from the physics which one the question wants. Second, speed and velocity are not interchangeable. The speed at any height is the same going up as coming down, by symmetry and by energy conservation, but the velocity differs because the vertical component has reversed sign. A ball thrown upward at 20 metres per second returns to the thrower's hand at 20 metres per second downward, which is why catching it hurts as much as throwing it. Energy offers a useful cross check. Without drag the sum of kinetic and gravitational potential energy is constant, so one half m v squared plus m g h does not change along the path. Any answer implying the projectile is faster at the top of its arc than at launch is wrong.

sections.heading: Deriving the Parabola and Reading Its Shape
sections.body: The trajectory equation is obtained by eliminating time between the two position equations. From the horizontal relation, t equals x divided by v cos theta. Substituting into the vertical relation gives y equals x tan theta minus g x squared divided by twice the square of v cos theta. This is a quadratic in x with a negative coefficient on the squared term, which is the definition of a downward opening parabola. Every ideal trajectory is therefore a parabola, and every parabola with a vertical axis can be produced by some launch speed and angle. Reading the equation teaches more than deriving it. The first term, x tan theta, is the straight line the projectile would follow if gravity were switched off, the so called line of departure. The second term is the drop below that line, and it depends on x squared but not at all on theta except through the cos squared factor. This is the geometric statement of the monkey and hunter result: the shortfall below the aiming line is a pure function of flight time, and therefore of horizontal distance for a given speed. The vertex of the parabola sits at the apex of the flight, where the vertical velocity is momentarily zero. At that instant the projectile is still moving at v cos theta horizontally, so it is not motionless; a common misconception has the object pausing in mid air. The horizontal position of the apex is exactly half the range on level ground, and the curve is symmetric about a vertical line through it. That symmetry has a practical corollary: the descent angle at the landing point on level ground equals the launch angle, and the impact speed equals the launch speed. The curvature of the path is greatest at the apex and least at the steep ends, which is a consequence of gravity being wholly perpendicular to the velocity at the top and largely parallel to it near the ends. Curvature relates to the component of acceleration perpendicular to the velocity, and at the apex all of g is perpendicular. This is why lofted shots look flat near their tops even when the whole trajectory is steep, and why a high mortar shell seems to hang. One elegant construction summarises everything. If you draw the line of departure and mark equal intervals of horizontal distance along it, then hang from each mark a vertical segment whose length grows as the square of the number of intervals, the lower ends of those segments trace the trajectory. The lengths run one, four, nine, sixteen units, which is Galileo's odd number rule expressed cumulatively. A gunner with a ruler and no algebra can plot a usable trajectory this way in a few minutes, which is essentially how early fire control tables were drawn before analytical methods became routine.

sections.heading: Range, Height, Time of Flight, and the Envelope of Safety
sections.body: For a launch and landing at the same height, three results follow immediately and are worth committing to memory. The time of flight is twice the initial vertical velocity divided by g, that is 2 v sin theta over g, because the rise and the fall take equal times. The maximum height is the square of the initial vertical velocity divided by twice g, that is v squared sin squared theta over 2 g. The horizontal range is the constant horizontal velocity multiplied by the time of flight, which simplifies using a trigonometric identity to v squared sin of twice theta, all divided by g. Put numbers on it. A ball thrown at 20 metres per second at 30 degrees has a vertical component of 10 and a horizontal component of 17.3 metres per second. It rises for 1.02 seconds to a height of 5.1 metres, flies for 2.04 seconds in total, and lands 35.3 metres away. Double the launch speed to 40 metres per second and the range quadruples to 141 metres, because range scales as the square of speed. This quadratic dependence is the single most important scaling in the subject. It is why a modest increase in muzzle velocity buys a disproportionate increase in reach, why bowlers and pitchers are trained relentlessly for release speed, and why a 10 per cent error in an estimated throwing speed produces a 20 per cent error in the predicted landing point. Height scales as the square of speed too, but the time of flight scales only linearly. A projectile fired twice as fast at the same angle is in the air twice as long and covers four times the ground. On the Moon, where g is 1.62 metres per second squared, the same throw would go about six times as far and stay aloft six times as long, which is why the golf shot Alan Shepard attempted in 1971 was so widely misjudged; his stiff pressure suit, not the gravity, limited it. A less familiar but very useful result is the envelope of safety. Fire from one point at fixed speed v in every possible direction, and the family of all resulting parabolas has a boundary beyond which nothing can reach. That boundary is itself a parabola, described by y equals v squared over 2 g minus g x squared over 2 v squared. Its apex is at height v squared over 2 g directly overhead, which is exactly the height a vertical shot would reach, and it meets the ground at the maximum range v squared over g. Any target inside the envelope can be hit by two different launch angles; a target exactly on it by one; a target outside it by none. Artillery officers call the two solutions the low angle and high angle options, and the choice between them is a tactical decision about flight time, terrain masking, and descent angle rather than about whether the shot is possible.

sections.heading: Optimal Angles, Complementary Pairs, and Launching from a Height
sections.body: Because the range on level ground is proportional to the sine of twice the launch angle, and the sine function peaks at 90 degrees, the range is greatest when twice the angle equals 90 degrees, that is at 45 degrees. This is the most quoted result in the subject and also the most frequently misapplied, because it holds only in a vacuum and only when the launch and landing heights are equal. An immediate corollary is that angles adding to 90 degrees give identical ranges. Thirty and sixty degrees both produce sin of 60 degrees, so both send a projectile the same distance by very different routes. The 30 degree shot is flat and quick; the 60 degree shot is high and long in duration, arriving steeply.
