At 20 metres per second both reach 35.3 metres, but the low shot takes 2.04 seconds and peaks at 5.1 metres while the high shot takes 3.53 seconds and peaks at 15.3 metres. Choosing between them is choosing between exposure time, clearance over obstacles, and the angle at which the projectile arrives. Mortars exist to exploit the high solution, dropping rounds behind walls and ridges that a flat trajectory cannot pass. The 45 degree rule fails as soon as the launch point is above or below the landing point. Throwing from a height gives the projectile extra fall time for free, and that extra time is more valuable if spent moving horizontally, so the optimum angle drops below 45 degrees. The optimum for a launch from height h at speed v satisfies sin squared of the optimal angle equals v squared divided by twice the quantity v squared plus g h. Thrown at 15 metres per second from a 20 metre cliff, the optimum is about 33 degrees, not 45, and using 45 degrees costs several metres of range. In shot put, where the implement is released from roughly two metres above the ground at around 13 metres per second, the theoretical optimum is near 42 degrees; in practice elite throwers release between 34 and 38 degrees because the human body cannot generate the same release speed at steeper angles, and speed matters more than angle. That trade off, where the biomechanically achievable speed falls as the angle rises, is the real reason almost no sporting technique uses 45 degrees. Launching from below the landing point reverses the correction: the optimum angle rises above 45 degrees, because extra height must be bought with vertical velocity before any horizontal progress counts. Javelin and long jump complicate matters further because the implement or body generates aerodynamic lift, and the optimum angles fall to roughly 32 to 36 degrees for javelin and around 20 degrees for a long jump takeoff. Jumping at 45 degrees would demand a vertical velocity no sprinter can produce in the fraction of a second board contact allows, and would destroy the horizontal speed that dominates the result. The lesson is that 45 degrees answers one specific idealised question, and treating it as universal is among the commonest bad transfers of a physics result into a context that cannot support it.

sections.heading: Worked Examples from Everyday Scales to Artillery
sections.body: Consider first a fire hose. Water leaves a nozzle at 25 metres per second, held at 40 degrees, from a height of 1.5 metres. The components are 19.15 horizontal and 16.07 vertical. Ignoring air resistance, the vertical position is 1.5 plus 16.07 t minus 4.905 t squared, which reaches zero at t equal to 3.36 seconds. Multiplying by the horizontal component gives a reach of 64 metres. Real hose streams fall well short of this, typically by 30 to 40 per cent, because the jet breaks into droplets that are decelerated severely by air; fire service reach tables are empirical for exactly this reason, and the calculation serves only as an upper bound. Second, a basketball free throw. The hoop is 3.05 metres high and 4.6 metres from the line, and a player releases from about 2.1 metres, so the ball must rise 0.95 metres over 4.6 metres of travel. Any of a family of speed and angle pairs will do, but the entry angle matters more than the trajectory, because a ball entering steeply sees a larger effective opening. The hoop is 0.45 metres across and the ball 0.24 metres, so a horizontal entry would need an impossible alignment while an entry near 45 degrees leaves comfortable margin. Coaching guidance converges on release angles of 50 to 55 degrees at roughly 7 metres per second, which is a good illustration of the target geometry, not the range formula, setting the optimum. Third, a level artillery problem. A shell leaves at 800 metres per second at 20 degrees. Ideal components are 751.8 horizontal and 273.6 vertical. Time of flight would be 55.8 seconds, apex 3,816 metres, range 41.9 kilometres. Actual field guns of that muzzle velocity reach roughly 20 to 24 kilometres. The vacuum answer is out by nearly a factor of two, which is the clearest possible demonstration that above a few hundred metres per second drag is not a correction but the main event. The flight is also long enough that the shell climbs into thinner air, that the Earth turns beneath it by several tens of metres, and that gravity itself is measurably weaker at apex. Fourth, a reconstruction. A vehicle leaves a horizontal cliff edge and is found 18 metres out and 7 metres down. The fall time is the square root of two times 7 divided by 9.81, which is 1.195 seconds. The horizontal speed is therefore 18 divided by 1.195, about 15.1 metres per second, or 54 kilometres per hour. Because a car is bluff and slow enough for drag to be modest over such a short flight, this estimate is usually quoted with an uncertainty of a few kilometres per hour and is admissible in court. The same method run in reverse tells a jumper how fast they must be travelling to clear a gap, and the honest answer is almost always faster than they expect.

sections.heading: Air Resistance: The Linear and Quadratic Regimes
sections.body: Air resistance is a force opposing motion through a fluid, and its magnitude depends on speed in one of two broadly different ways depending on how the air flows around the object. For very small or very slow objects the flow is smooth and layered, and the drag is proportional to speed. This is Stokes drag, and for a sphere it equals six pi times the fluid viscosity times the radius times the speed. It governs mist droplets, pollen, dust and the settling of silt in water. For anything larger or faster, the flow behind the object separates and becomes turbulent, and the drag becomes proportional to the square of the speed, equal to one half times the air density times the drag coefficient times the frontal area times the speed squared. The dividing line is set by the Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial to viscous effects, computed as density times speed times diameter divided by viscosity. Below about one, drag is linear. Above a few thousand, drag is firmly quadratic. A cricket ball at 30 metres per second has a Reynolds number near 150,000 and is deeply in the quadratic regime; a 20 micrometre dust grain drifting at a centimetre per second is at 0.013 and firmly in the linear one. Almost every projectile a person deals with is quadratic, which is unfortunate because the linear case has a tidy analytic solution and the quadratic case does not. The linear case is worth understanding anyway because it is solvable and shows the qualitative behaviour. With drag proportional to velocity, the horizontal velocity decays exponentially towards zero with a time constant equal to mass divided by the drag constant, and the horizontal distance approaches a finite asymptote no matter how long the flight. The vertical motion approaches a constant terminal velocity. The trajectory is therefore not a parabola but a curve that rises to a rounded apex and then descends increasingly steeply, eventually falling almost vertically. That shape is exactly the one drawn in the medieval gunnery manuals, which is a pleasing vindication of empirical observation over idealised theory. The quadratic case has no closed form solution in general and must be integrated numerically, but its characteristic parameter is the terminal velocity, the speed at which drag balances weight. It equals the square root of twice the mass times g divided by the product of air density, drag coefficient and frontal area. A person in a stable belly to earth skydiving posture has a terminal velocity near 55 metres per second; head down it rises to about 90. A baseball is near 40 metres per second, a table tennis ball around 9, a raindrop of two millimetres about 6.5, and a large hailstone can exceed 40. As a rule of thumb, if a projectile's launch speed is well below its terminal velocity, drag is a modest correction and the parabola is a decent guide. If launch speed approaches or exceeds terminal velocity, the parabola is simply the wrong shape and using it will mislead badly.

sections.heading: Solving Real Trajectories: Numerical Integration and Ballistic Coefficients
sections.body: Once drag varies as the square of the speed, the equations of motion couple the horizontal and vertical components together and no elementary function solves them. The practical response is to step the solution forward in small time increments. In the simplest scheme, due to Euler, you compute the total speed, work out the drag force, resolve it opposite to the velocity direction, add gravity, divide by mass to get the acceleration, and then update velocity and position by multiplying by a small time step. Repeat until the projectile reaches the ground. The scheme is easy to implement on any calculator or in twenty lines of code, but it accumulates error in a predictable direction: it consistently overestimates because it applies the acceleration at the start of the interval to the whole interval. Halving the step size halves the error, which means acceptable accuracy demands very small steps. Better schemes evaluate the acceleration at several points within the step and combine them. The midpoint method uses two evaluations and its error falls with the square of the step size; the classical fourth order Runge Kutta method uses four and its error falls with the fourth power, so halving the step reduces error sixteenfold. For a rifle bullet, fourth order Runge Kutta with a one millisecond step is more than adequate over any practical range. Practitioners rarely carry drag coefficients around. Instead ballistics uses the ballistic coefficient, a single number expressing how well a projectile retains speed compared with a standard reference shape. The most common references are the G1 model, a flat based blunt nosed form dating from late nineteenth century work at the Gavre commission in France, and the G7 model, a modern boat tailed secant ogive that matches long range rifle bullets far better. A bullet with a G7 ballistic coefficient of 0.300 loses velocity at the same proportional rate as the G7 standard projectile scaled to that value. Because the drag coefficient of any real shape varies strongly with Mach number, particularly through the transonic band from roughly Mach 0.8 to 1.2 where shock waves form and drag can double, a single coefficient is only an approximation. Quoting a G1 coefficient for a sleek modern bullet is a known source of error at long range, and mixing the two conventions is a classic and expensive mistake. The transonic region deserves respect for another reason. As a supersonic projectile decelerates through the speed of sound, roughly 343 metres per second at 20 degrees Celsius but varying with temperature, the shock structure reorganises and the centre of pressure shifts. Long range marksmen often observe that groups open up dramatically once bullets go subsonic, and the usual remedy is to choose a load that keeps the bullet supersonic all the way to the target. Air density matters too: it falls by about 12 per cent per thousand metres of altitude, so the same rifle zeroed at sea level shoots noticeably flatter in the mountains, and cold dense air at minus 10 degrees Celsius produces measurably more drop than warm thin air at plus 30.

sections.heading: Spin, the Magnus Effect, and Trajectories That Curve Sideways
sections.body: A spinning object moving through air experiences a force perpendicular to both its axis of spin and its direction of travel. This is the Magnus effect, named for Heinrich Gustav Magnus who described it in 1852, though Newton had noted the curved flight of cut tennis balls at Cambridge in 1672 and Benjamin Robins demonstrated musket ball deflection in the 1740s. The mechanism is that the spinning surface drags a thin layer of air with it, so on one side the surface motion adds to the airflow and on the other it opposes it. The boundary layer separates later on the fast side and earlier on the slow side, which deflects the wake to one side, and by conservation of momentum the ball is pushed the other way. The magnitude is respectable. A football struck with heavy sidespin at 25 metres per second and spinning at 10 revolutions per second can be deflected several metres over a 30 metre flight, which is the physics of a curling free kick. Backspin on a golf ball, typically 50 to 100 revolutions per second immediately after a driver strike, produces an upward Magnus force that can be a substantial fraction of the ball's weight, extending carry by tens of metres compared with a non spinning ball. The dimples are not decorative: by tripping the boundary layer into turbulence they delay separation, cutting pressure drag roughly in half at typical speeds and simultaneously strengthening the Magnus response. A smooth ball struck identically would travel less than half as far. Topspin does the opposite, pressing the ball down and allowing a tennis player or table tennis player to hit much harder while still landing the ball inside the court. The characteristic dipping forehand of the modern topspin game exists entirely because of this. In cricket, swing bowling uses a related but distinct mechanism: the seam is angled and the ball polished on one side only, so the boundary layer becomes turbulent on one face and laminar on the other, generating a side force without much spin at all. Reverse swing at high speeds occurs when both sides go turbulent but at different points, flipping the direction. Baseball's knuckleball is the inverse trick. Thrown with almost no rotation, the ball's raised seams sit in one orientation long enough for the wake to lock into an asymmetric pattern, then the pattern flips as the ball creeps around, producing erratic and genuinely unpredictable deflections. It is one of the few sporting techniques whose whole value is that neither the batter nor the pitcher can predict the trajectory. For projectiles fired from rifled barrels, spin serves a different purpose: gyroscopic stabilisation against tumbling. A side effect is spin drift, a steady lateral drift of the order of 20 to 30 centimetres at 1,000 metres for a right hand twist, caused by the gyroscopic response to the bullet's nose tracking slightly above the trajectory. Long range shooters must account for it separately from wind.

sections.heading: The Rotating Earth: Coriolis, Eötvös, and Very Long Shots
sections.body: For flights of a few seconds the Earth may be treated as a flat, stationary platform. For flights of tens of seconds and ranges of tens of kilometres it cannot, and two additional effects appear. Both are consequences of working in a rotating reference frame rather than of any new force acting on the projectile. The Coriolis effect deflects anything moving over the Earth's surface, to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. The acceleration equals twice the Earth's rotation rate, 7.292 times ten to the minus five radians per second, multiplied by the component of velocity perpendicular to the rotation axis, and it therefore scales with latitude through the sine of the latitude for horizontal deflection. The deflection grows roughly as the square of the flight time, so it is negligible for a thrown ball and decisive for a shell. A 155 millimetre howitzer firing 25 kilometres at 50 degrees north puts the round about 60 to 80 metres to the right of the aiming line, which is far larger than the weapon's dispersion. Modern fire control computers apply the correction automatically; before they existed it was tabulated by latitude and azimuth. The much repeated claim that the British squadron at the Battle of the Falkland Islands in December 1914 missed because their tables were calibrated for the northern hemisphere and the deflection reversed at 52 degrees south is a good story that historians treat with caution. The gunnery records show many other causes of inaccuracy, including funnel smoke and rangefinding at extreme range, and the doubled Coriolis error of a few hundred metres would have been one contributor among several. It is worth telling as an illustration of the effect's size, not as settled history. The related claim that the Coriolis effect determines which way water drains from a bath is simply false; the effect is many orders of magnitude weaker than the residual swirl left in the water. The Eötvös effect, named for the Hungarian physicist Loránd Eötvös who identified it from shipborne gravity measurements around 1900, changes the effective vertical acceleration depending on whether the projectile travels eastward or westward. Moving east adds to the Earth's rotational velocity, increasing the centrifugal contribution and slightly reducing effective gravity, so an eastward shot flies marginally further; a westward shot falls slightly shorter. The difference is a few tenths of a per cent at typical artillery speeds, small but not zero at 40 kilometres. Three further refinements matter at extreme range. Gravity weakens with altitude, so a shell reaching 10 kilometres apex experiences about 0.3 per cent less gravity there. Air density falls roughly exponentially with a scale height near 8.5 kilometres, so high trajectories spend much of their flight in thin air and travel further than a constant density model predicts. And the Earth curves away beneath the trajectory, so the ground is lower at the target than a flat model assumes, adding range. The Paris Gun of 1918, firing 120 kilometres with a 40 kilometre apex, was designed around exactly these effects and could not have been aimed without them.

sections.heading: Practical Ballistics: Zeroing, Holdover, and Reading the Wind
sections.body: A sighting device sits above the bore of a firearm, typically 4 to 6 centimetres for a telescopic sight, and points along a straight line. The projectile follows a curve that begins below that line, crosses it on the way up, arcs above it, and crosses it again on the way down. Zeroing means choosing the barrel elevation so that the second crossing occurs at a chosen distance. A rifle zeroed at 200 metres is therefore also very nearly on target at about 25 metres, where the first crossing occurs, and shoots a few centimetres high in between. This near zero and far zero pair is the single most useful thing a shooter can internalise, because it converts a curved trajectory into a usable flat band. The concept of point blank range follows: it is the span over which the projectile stays within some acceptable vertical window, often taken as plus or minus 5 centimetres for a small target. A typical centrefire rifle cartridge zeroed sensibly gives a point blank span from the muzzle to roughly 250 to 300 metres, within which no elevation adjustment is needed at all. Beyond that, holdover or a dialled correction becomes necessary and grows rapidly, because drop accumulates as the square of flight time. Angular units make the corrections manageable. One milliradian subtends 10 centimetres at 100 metres and 1 metre at 1,000 metres, which makes mental arithmetic trivial. One minute of angle subtends about 2.9 centimetres at 100 metres, commonly rounded to one inch at 100 yards. Reticles marked in milliradians allow a shooter both to estimate range from a target of known size and to apply corrections in the same units, which is why they dominate long range practice. Wind is usually the dominant uncertainty beyond a few hundred metres, and it is widely misunderstood. Wind does not simply push the bullet sideways for the flight duration. The correct quantity is lag time, the difference between the actual flight time and the time a drag free projectile would have taken. Wind deflection equals the crosswind speed multiplied by that lag. This is why deflection grows faster than linearly with range, and why a bullet that has slowed markedly is far more wind sensitive than its starting velocity suggests. A 10 kilometre per hour full value crosswind might move a typical rifle bullet 7 centimetres at 300 metres but 90 centimetres at 900 metres. Wind rarely blows squarely across the line of fire, so shooters resolve it by clock position, taking the full value at 3 and 9 o'clock, roughly 87 per cent at 2, 4, 8 and 10 o'clock, and half value at 1, 5, 7 and 11 o'clock. Wind near the shooter matters more than wind near the target, because a deflection applied early has the whole remaining flight to accumulate lateral distance. Reading mirage through a spotting scope, watching vegetation, and noting that valleys channel and accelerate wind are all part of the craft, and none of it can be replaced by calculation because the atmosphere between the two points is not uniform.

sections.heading: Measuring and Predicting a Trajectory in the Field
sections.body: Predicting where something will land requires only the launch speed, the launch angle and the launch height, plus a decision about how much drag matters. All can be measured with improvised equipment to useful accuracy, and doing so is instructive because the discrepancy between prediction and outcome is itself the measurement of drag. The most accessible speed measurement uses the trajectory in reverse. Launch the object horizontally from a measured height and note where it lands. From a table 1.20 metres high the fall time is the square root of two times 1.20 over 9.81, or 0.495 seconds, so an object landing 3.40 metres out left at 6.87 metres per second. Because the flight is short, drag contributes little and the estimate is good to a few per cent for dense compact objects. Repeat five times and use the mean; the spread is your honest uncertainty, typically 5 to 10 per cent by hand. For angles, a smartphone inclinometer or a protractor with a plumb line taped to the launcher is adequate. Angles are easier to set than speeds, and errors in them matter less near the optimum, because range depends on the sine of twice the angle, whose derivative vanishes at 45 degrees. Two degrees of error at 45 degrees costs 0.1 per cent of range; the same error at 15 degrees costs 4 per cent. Anything with a low mass to frontal area ratio falls far short of the vacuum prediction. A ping pong ball, a foam dart or a shuttlecock may achieve half or less of the calculated range, while dense compact objects launched below about 20 metres per second usually land within 5 to 15 per cent of prediction. Expressing the shortfall as a percentage characterises drag empirically without computing a drag coefficient.
steps: Choose a flat, clear run of ground at least twice your expected range, with nobody downrange and no windows or roads in the fall zone.
Measure the launch height from the ground to the point at which the object leaves the launcher, not to the launcher's base.
Set the launch angle with an inclinometer or a plumb line protractor clamped to the launch axis, and record it to the nearest degree.
Determine launch speed by firing horizontally from a known height and measuring the distance to first impact, repeating at least five times.
Compute the fall time as the square root of twice the launch height divided by 9.81, then divide the mean horizontal distance by that time.
Predict the range as launch speed squared times the sine of twice the angle, divided by 9.81.
Mark the predicted landing point with a peg before firing, so the comparison is honest and not adjusted afterwards.
Fire five shots at the chosen angle, marking each impact, and record the mean distance and the spread.
Express the shortfall as a percentage of the prediction; this is your empirical drag correction at that speed.
Repeat at a second angle and speed to check whether the correction is stable; expect it to grow as launch speed rises.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits of the Model, and What to Do When It Goes Wrong
sections.body: The commonest failure is applying the vacuum parabola outside its domain. The model is trustworthy when the projectile is dense, compact, slow relative to its terminal velocity, not spinning appreciably, and in flight for a short time. It becomes unreliable in proportion to how many of those conditions are broken. A good habit is to compute the terminal velocity before trusting any prediction: if launch speed exceeds about a third of terminal velocity, expect errors above 10 per cent, and if it exceeds terminal velocity, expect the calculated range to be wildly optimistic. The 42 kilometre versus 22 kilometre artillery discrepancy is the extreme case, but a foam dart, a shuttlecock or a light plastic ball fails just as badly at walking pace. The second failure is sign and geometry error. Mixing an upward positive axis with a positive value for g, forgetting that a launch below the target means the vertical displacement is positive, or using the range formula when the landing height differs from the launch height, all produce answers that look plausible and are wrong. The defence is to sketch the situation, mark the origin, and state the sign of g explicitly before writing an equation. If a quadratic in time produces one positive and one negative root, the negative root corresponds to the projectile's imaginary past before launch and should be discarded, not treated as an error. The third failure is treating averages as exact. Real launches scatter. Hand thrown speeds vary by several per cent shot to shot, wind changes between shots, and small differences in release angle compound. Any single prediction should be quoted with a range, and the sensible way to obtain it is to recompute with the launch speed varied by the observed scatter. Because range depends on the square of speed, a 5 per cent speed uncertainty becomes a 10 per cent range uncertainty, and this dominates almost every other source of error in practical work. The fourth failure is misreading what the model is for. Predicting exactly where a shell lands from first principles is nearly hopeless; every serious ballistics practice uses tables or software calibrated against live firing, and then applies corrections for the day's temperature, pressure, wind and propellant lot. The physics tells you which variables matter and how strongly, which is what allows a correction to be applied intelligently, but the absolute numbers come from measurement. When a prediction and an outcome disagree, work through the causes in order of typical magnitude. Check launch speed first, because it is squared and is usually the least well known quantity. Check drag second, by asking whether the object is light for its size. Check the launch and landing heights third, because a height difference is frequently overlooked. Check wind fourth. Only then consider spin, and only for very long flights consider the rotation of the Earth. Working the list in this order finds the culprit quickly, and resisting the temptation to reach for the exotic explanation before the mundane one is the mark of someone who has done this before.

guides.safetyNote: Any physical trial of these principles launches something at speed. Establish a clear fall zone at least twice the predicted range, keep everyone behind the launch line, wear eye protection, and never aim a launcher at a person, an animal or a road even when you believe it cannot reach them, because launch speeds scatter and ranges depend on the square of speed.

guides.title: Motion, Forces & Newton's Laws
guides.summary: How and why objects move: the vocabulary of motion (position, velocity, acceleration), Newton's three laws, the common forces (gravity, normal, friction, tension), momentum, and how to solve real problems with free-body diagrams and worked examples.

sections.heading: The language of motion: displacement, velocity, acceleration
sections.body:
Mechanics splits into two halves that are easy to confuse. Kinematics describes motion — where something is, how fast it is going, how that is changing — without asking what causes it. Dynamics explains motion by bringing in forces. Every mechanics problem becomes easier once the description is nailed down first, and that means defining four quantities with more care than everyday speech allows.

Position, written x, is where an object sits along a chosen axis, measured from an origin you select, in metres. It is a vector quantity, carrying direction as well as size; along a single line that direction is encoded entirely in the sign. Displacement, written as delta-x and equal to the final position minus the initial position, is the straight-line change in position. It is not the same thing as distance. Distance is the total length of path travelled and can never be negative, whereas displacement can be zero after a long journey. An athlete running one full lap of a 400 m track covers a distance of 400 m and a displacement of exactly zero, because they finish where they began.

Velocity is the rate at which position changes: velocity equals change in position divided by change in time, measured in metres per second. It too is a vector, so 60 km/h north is a different velocity from 60 km/h south even though both correspond to the same speed. Speed is the magnitude of velocity with the direction stripped away, and is never negative. Average velocity uses total displacement over total time; instantaneous velocity is the limit of that ratio as the time interval shrinks toward zero, which is what a speedometer approximates.

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, in metres per second squared. Those units repay a moment's thought — metres per second, per second — meaning an acceleration of 3 m/s squared adds 3 m/s to the velocity every second that passes. Because velocity is a vector, acceleration occurs whenever the speed changes or the direction changes or both. A car rounding a bend at a steady 50 km/h is accelerating continuously even though the speedometer never moves. Negative acceleration does not automatically mean slowing down, either: it means the acceleration points in the negative direction, which slows an object travelling positively but speeds up one already travelling negatively.

The single most valuable habit is fixing a sign convention before writing anything down and then refusing to change it. Declare which direction counts as positive — up, or east, or forward — and let the algebra carry the physics. Throw a ball upward at 15 m/s with up positive, and gravity supplies an acceleration of minus 9.8 m/s squared. The equations then deliver, with no further thought required, a velocity that falls to zero at the peak and grows increasingly negative on the way down. That minus sign is doing real work, and most sign errors in mechanics trace back to quietly redefining positive partway through a problem.

sections.heading: The kinematic equations for constant acceleration
sections.body:
When acceleration is constant, five quantities describe the motion completely: the initial velocity u, the final velocity v, the acceleration a, the elapsed time t, and the displacement s. Four standard equations connect them, and each deliberately omits one variable, which makes choosing between them straightforward — pick the equation that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor want.

The first is v = u + a·t, which omits displacement and follows directly from the definition of acceleration rearranged. The second is s = u·t + ½·a·t², which omits the final velocity. The third is v² = u² + 2·a·s, which omits time altogether and is the workhorse for any question phrased in terms of distance rather than duration. The fourth is s = ½·(u + v)·t, which omits acceleration and states simply that displacement equals average velocity multiplied by time — a relation that holds only because uniform acceleration makes the mean of the initial and final velocities the true average.

Units must be consistent throughout: velocities in metres per second, acceleration in metres per second squared, time in seconds, displacement in metres. Mixing kilometres per hour into an equation expecting metres per second is the commonest arithmetic failure in the whole subject; the conversion is division by 3.6, so 72 km/h is 20 m/s.

The constant-acceleration condition is a genuine restriction rather than a formality. These equations are exact for free fall near the Earth's surface with air resistance neglected, where a = g of about 9.8 m/s², and for constant-thrust or steady-braking problems. They are simply wrong for a car accelerating from rest under a real engine, whose acceleration falls off through the gears, or for a skydiver whose drag grows with speed until it balances weight. Those cases need calculus or step-by-step numerical methods.

A worked braking example shows the method in full. A car travels at u = 20 m/s and brakes at a = −5 m/s². For the stopping distance, the final velocity is zero and time is unwanted, so the third equation applies: 0² = 20² + 2(−5)s, giving 0 = 400 − 10s, so s = 40 m. For the stopping time, the first equation gives 0 = 20 + (−5)t, so t = 4 s.

That result carries a lesson worth more than the arithmetic. Because velocity appears squared in the third equation, stopping distance scales with the square of speed. Doubling from 20 m/s to 40 m/s does not double the 40 m stopping distance — it quadruples it, to 160 m. This is exactly the relationship behind published stopping-distance tables and the reason modest changes in speed limits have a disproportionate effect on collision severity. Real tables add thinking distance too: roughly 0.7 to 1.5 seconds of reaction time before the brakes are even touched, during which the car covers ground at its full original speed.

sections.heading: Newton's First Law — inertia
sections.body:
Newton's First Law states that an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues at constant velocity — the same speed in the same straight line — unless acted upon by a net external force. Two words in that sentence carry most of the weight. Net means the vector sum of every force acting: a book resting on a table has gravity pulling it down and the table pushing it up, and because those cancel exactly, the net force is zero and the book stays where it is. External means a force exerted by something outside the object, since nothing can accelerate itself through internal forces alone.

The property the law describes is inertia, the tendency of matter to resist changes in its state of motion, and mass in kilograms is its quantitative measure. A loaded lorry is harder to start and harder to stop than a bicycle, not because gravity treats it differently but because it has more inertia. Mass in this sense — inertial mass — is conceptually distinct from the gravitational mass that determines weight, and the experimental finding that the two are identical to better than one part in ten trillion is one of the deepest facts in physics and the starting point for general relativity.

The counterintuitive content of the law is that no force at all is required to keep something moving. A hockey puck on frictionless ice would glide forever. On real surfaces friction is always quietly present, decelerating anything not actively pushed, and for roughly fourteen centuries that observation propped up Aristotle's contrary claim that motion requires a continuous mover. Galileo broke it with inclined planes: a ball rolled down one ramp climbs an opposing ramp back toward its starting height, and as the surfaces are made smoother it climbs closer and closer to that height whatever the second ramp's angle. Extrapolate the second ramp to horizontal and the ball never stops at all.

The everyday consequences are immediate. A passenger lurches forward when a car brakes hard, because the passenger's inertia keeps them moving at the original speed while the vehicle decelerates beneath them; a seatbelt exists precisely to supply the force that decelerates the passenger at the same rate as the car, over the same distance. A tablecloth can be pulled from beneath crockery because the frictional force, though real, acts for too short a time to change the crockery's motion appreciably. A headrest addresses the mirror-image case in a rear-end impact, when the seat accelerates the torso forward and the unsupported head is left behind.

The law also defines the reference frames in which the rest of mechanics is valid. A frame in which a genuinely force-free object moves at constant velocity is called inertial. An accelerating car, a braking train and a spinning roundabout are non-inertial frames, and inside them objects appear to accelerate with no identifiable cause — the sensation of being thrown outward on a fairground ride. Newton's laws in their simple form hold only in inertial frames.

sections.heading: Newton's Second Law — F = m·a
sections.body:
Newton's Second Law makes the first law quantitative: the net force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, written F_net = m·a. Every symbol needs care. F_net is the vector sum of all forces acting, in newtons; m is mass in kilograms; a is the resulting acceleration in metres per second squared. The newton is a derived unit defined by this very equation — one newton is the force that gives a one-kilogram mass an acceleration of one metre per second squared, so 1 N equals 1 kg·m/s². As a physical intuition, a newton is roughly the weight of a small apple.

Two properties follow at once. Force and acceleration always point the same way, because mass is a positive scalar, so an object can never accelerate in any direction other than that of the net force. And acceleration is inversely proportional to mass, so for a given push, doubling the mass halves the acceleration. Newton's own more general statement was framed in terms of momentum — force equals the rate of change of momentum — which reduces to F = ma whenever mass is constant and stays correct when it is not, as for a rocket steadily burning away its fuel.

A worked example fixes the procedure. Push a 50 kg crate across a floor with 200 N while friction resists with 80 N. The two forces oppose, so the net force is 200 minus 80, or 120 N, and the acceleration is 120 divided by 50, which is 2.4 m/s². Swap in a 100 kg crate and the same net force yields 120 divided by 100, or 1.2 m/s². Now push with only 80 N against 80 N of friction: the net force is zero, and the crate slides on at constant velocity — moving steadily, with a force clearly applied, and no acceleration whatsoever. That case is the everyday illusion underpinning the belief that motion needs a continuous push.

Weight is where the law is most often misapplied. Weight is a force, not an amount of matter, and equals mass times gravitational field strength: W = m·g, with g about 9.8 m/s², equivalently 9.8 newtons per kilogram. A 70 kg person weighs 70 times 9.8, or 686 N, on Earth. On the Moon, where g is about 1.62 m/s², that same person still has 70 kg of mass but weighs only around 113 N. A bathroom scale actually measures force and then divides by an assumed value of g to display kilograms, which is precisely why it would read incorrectly on the Moon. Confusing the two quantities is the single most frequent error in introductory mechanics.

One consequence is worth isolating. In free fall the only force acting is weight, so the acceleration is W divided by m, which is m·g divided by m, which is simply g — independent of mass. The mass cancels exactly. That cancellation is why, with air resistance removed, everything falls at the same rate.

sections.heading: Newton's Third Law — action and reaction
sections.body:
Newton's Third Law states that if body A exerts a force on body B, then body B exerts a force on body A of equal magnitude and opposite direction. Forces, in other words, never occur singly; they always come in pairs. The decisive detail, and the one that dissolves almost every confusion about this law, is that the two members of a pair act on different objects. They therefore can never cancel each other, because cancellation only means anything between forces acting on the same body.

Three examples make the mechanism concrete. Walking works because your foot pushes backward against the ground through friction and the ground pushes forward on your foot with an equal force; that reaction is what propels you, which is why walking on frictionless ice is impossible however vigorously the legs move. A rocket expels exhaust gas downward at high speed and the gas pushes the rocket upward with an equal force — and this works perfectly in vacuum, because the rocket pushes against its own propellant rather than against any surrounding air. The New York Times editorialised otherwise about Robert Goddard in 1920 and printed a retraction in 1969 as Apollo 11 was on its way to the Moon. A swimmer pushes water backward and the water pushes the swimmer forward.

Force pairs always share a type. If the action is gravitational, so is the reaction: the Earth pulls a 1 kg apple down with about 9.8 N, and the apple pulls the Earth up with exactly 9.8 N. The apple accelerates at 9.8 m/s², while the Earth accelerates at 9.8 N divided by its mass of about 6 times 10 to the 24th kilograms, roughly a millionth of a billionth of a billionth of a metre per second squared. Equal forces, wildly unequal accelerations, because the second law divides by mass.

The standard objection deserves a full answer: if forces always come in equal and opposite pairs, how does anything ever accelerate? Take a horse pulling a cart. The horse pulls the cart forward and the cart pulls the horse backward with equal force, but those act on different bodies and cannot legitimately be added. To ask whether the cart accelerates, analyse the cart alone — forward harness tension against backward rolling friction. If tension exceeds friction, it accelerates. To ask whether the horse accelerates, analyse the horse alone — the backward pull of the harness against the forward friction of the ground beneath its hooves.

That is the general rule, and the reason free-body analysis exists: draw a boundary around exactly one object and count only the forces crossing that boundary. A related trap is treating a book's weight and the table's normal force as a third-law pair. They are not. They act on the same object, they are different kinds of force, and they are equal only because the book happens not to be accelerating. The genuine partner of the book's weight is the book's own gravitational pull on the Earth.

sections.heading: The everyday forces and free-body diagrams
sections.body:
Real problems combine a handful of standard forces, and the reliable route to a solution is the free-body diagram: a sketch of one chosen object, reduced to a dot or a simple box, with every force acting on it drawn as an arrow pointing outward, labelled and roughly to scale. Forces that the object exerts on other things never appear on its own diagram.

Weight is the gravitational pull of the Earth, equal to mass times g and always directed toward the Earth's centre, which at any human scale means straight down regardless of the slope underfoot. On an inclined plane it is normally resolved into a component along the slope, mg·sinθ, and one perpendicular to it, mg·cosθ.

The normal force is the perpendicular push a surface exerts on whatever rests against it, arising physically from microscopic compression of the surface material. It is a constraint force that adjusts itself to whatever value prevents interpenetration. On level ground with no vertical acceleration it equals weight, but that equality is a result rather than a definition: press down on a book and the normal force rises; accelerate upward in a lift and the floor pushes on you harder than your weight, which is exactly the sensation of feeling heavy as the lift starts.

Friction acts parallel to the contact surface and opposes relative sliding. Kinetic friction, once sliding has begun, equals μ_k times the normal force, while the maximum static friction before sliding starts equals μ_s times the normal force. The coefficient is dimensionless and belongs to the pairing of materials rather than to either one alone — roughly 0.6 to 0.9 for rubber on dry concrete, around 0.1 for a smooth sole on ice.

Tension is the pull transmitted along a rope, cable or chain, always directed along the rope and away from the object. An ideal rope, treated as massless and inextensible over a frictionless pulley, carries the same tension throughout, which is the approximation that makes pulley problems tractable. Ropes pull; they never push. Drag, spring forces and applied pushes complete the usual cast.

The procedure is fixed. Draw the free-body diagram for one object. Choose axes, tilting them along and perpendicular to any slope. Write the net force equal to mass times acceleration separately for each axis, remembering that acceleration perpendicular to a surface the object stays on is zero. Then solve.

A worked example: a 10 kg box on level ground is pulled by a horizontal rope at 40 N against kinetic friction with μ_k = 0.3. Vertically there is no acceleration, so the normal force equals the weight, 10 times 9.8, or 98 N. Friction is therefore 0.3 times 98, or 29.4 N. Horizontally the net force is 40 minus 29.4, or 10.6 N, giving an acceleration of 1.06 m/s². Had the rope instead pulled at 30 degrees above horizontal, its upward component would have reduced the normal force and with it the friction — a real effect deliberately exploited when dragging heavy loads.

sections.heading: Momentum, impulse and conservation
sections.body:
Momentum, written p, is mass multiplied by velocity, measured in kilogram-metres per second. It quantifies what Newton called the quantity of motion, and like velocity it is a vector, so direction and sign matter at every step. A 1,500 kg car at 20 m/s carries 30,000 kg·m/s of momentum; a 10 g bullet at 400 m/s carries 4 kg·m/s. Newton's own statement of the second law was in these terms: net force equals the rate of change of momentum.

That formulation leads straight to impulse. Rearranged, force multiplied by the time over which it acts equals the change in momentum, J = F·Δt = Δp, measured in newton-seconds, which are dimensionally identical to kg·m/s. The practical content is enormous. To bring a moving mass to rest you must remove a fixed quantity of momentum, set entirely by its mass and speed and not at all by how the stop is managed. What can be controlled is the time. Spread the same momentum change over a longer interval and the average force falls in exact proportion.

Essentially every piece of impact-protection engineering is an application of this. A car's crumple zone stretches a collision from perhaps 20 milliseconds to 100, cutting the peak force roughly fivefold. An airbag extends it further still and spreads the load over a larger area of the body. Bending your knees on landing, a boxer rolling with a punch, a gymnast's foam pit, packaging foam and dynamic climbing rope engineered to stretch all do precisely the same job. A numerical illustration: a 70 kg person moving at 14 m/s carries 980 kg·m/s. Stopped in 0.1 s, the average force is 9,800 N. Stopped in 0.5 s, it is 1,960 N. The survivability gap between those two figures is the entire subject of crash safety.

Conservation of momentum follows directly from the third law. In any interaction where no net external force acts on the system as a whole, total momentum before equals total momentum after: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂. Because the internal forces the two bodies exert on one another are equal, opposite, and act for exactly the same duration, the impulses they deliver cancel precisely.

A recoil example: a 3 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Before firing, total momentum is zero, so afterwards it must still be zero. That gives 0.010 times 400, plus 3 times the rifle's velocity, equals zero, so the rifle moves at about −1.33 m/s, backwards. The same principle governs rocket propulsion, billiard balls, spacecraft docking and the kick of a garden hose.

One caveat matters. Momentum is conserved in every collision, but kinetic energy is not. A collision in which the bodies stick together is perfectly inelastic and loses the maximum energy compatible with conserving momentum, that energy going into deformation, heat and sound. Elastic collisions, conserving both, are a fair approximation for billiard balls and an excellent one for gas molecules.

sections.heading: Projectile Motion: When Gravity Works in Two Dimensions at Once
sections.body:
Every projectile — a thrown ball, a diver leaving a platform, a crate pushed out the back of a relief aircraft — obeys one deceptively simple trick. With air resistance ignored, its horizontal and vertical motions are entirely independent and can be analysed as two separate one-dimensional problems running on the same clock. Horizontally no force acts along that axis, so the horizontal velocity never changes and x = v₀ₓ·t. Vertically gravity acts alone, so the constant-acceleration equations apply directly, with v_y = v₀y − g·t and y = v₀y·t − ½g·t². Time is the only thing linking the two.

That independence is not an approximation but a consequence of gravity pulling purely vertically. Its most famous demonstration is the simultaneous drop: a ball released from a table edge and a ball fired horizontally from the same height at the same instant strike the floor together, however fast the second is launched, because horizontal velocity has no bearing whatever on the vertical fall.

Take a humanitarian flight releasing a supply crate from 500 m while flying level at 60 m/s, about 216 km/h. The vertical fall alone sets the flight time: 500 = ½(9.8)t² gives t as the square root of 1000 divided by 9.8, roughly 10.1 s. Throughout that fall the crate keeps its forward speed, since nothing acts on it horizontally, so it travels 60 times 10.1, about 606 m beyond the release point. The crew must therefore let go more than half a kilometre short of the target, and a ten per cent error in estimated airspeed shifts the landing point by some 60 m — which is why aircrew work from computed release points rather than judgement.

For a projectile launched at angle θ above level ground and landing at the same height, two results are worth memorising. The time of flight is 2v₀sinθ/g and the range is v₀²sin(2θ)/g. Because sin(2θ) peaks when 2θ is 90 degrees, range is greatest at 45 degrees, and complementary angles such as 30 and 60 degrees give identical ranges. Maximum height is v₀²sin²θ divided by 2g.

Real projectiles depart from this, sometimes sharply. Air drag rises roughly with the square of speed and turns the symmetric parabola into an asymmetric curve with a steeper descent and a considerably shorter range; for a fast-moving ball the true range can be under half the vacuum prediction. Spin adds a sideways Magnus force, which is what bends a struck football and lifts a golf ball. And the neat 45-degree result assumes launch speed is independent of launch angle, which for a human body it is not. Mike Powell's 1991 long jump world record of 8.95 m left the board at roughly 20 to 24 degrees, because converting horizontal sprint speed into vertical lift costs speed, so the real optimum trades angle against the velocity still available at take-off.

sections.heading: Circular Motion and the Force That Keeps Things Turning
sections.body:
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is nonetheless accelerating — a fact that trips up almost everyone on first encounter, because constant speed sounds as though it ought to mean no acceleration. But acceleration is any change in velocity, and velocity is a vector carrying direction as well as magnitude. Travelling around a circle changes that direction continuously even when the speed never varies, and that demands a centripetal, or centre-seeking, acceleration pointed directly at the circle's centre, of size a_c = v²/r. By the second law such an acceleration requires a real physical force in the same direction, F_c = mv²/r, supplied by whatever happens to be available: tension in a string for a whirled ball, gravity for an orbiting satellite, the wall's normal force for a fairground rotor, and friction between tyre and road for a car on a bend.

Centripetal force is a role, not a new kind of force. Asking what the centripetal force is means asking which of the ordinary forces present is doing that job. If none of them can, the object simply travels straight on and leaves the curve.

The car case has real stakes. A car taking a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m/s, about 54 km/h, needs a_c = 225 divided by 50, which is 4.5 m/s². On a flat road only friction can supply it, and since the maximum friction available is μ times mg, the required coefficient of static friction is 4.5 divided by 9.8, roughly 0.46. Dry asphalt typically offers 0.7 to 0.9, a comfortable margin. Wet pavement can fall below 0.4 and ice far lower, which is precisely why a bend that is perfectly safe on a dry afternoon becomes a skid-off in rain: the force required has not changed, but the road's capacity to supply it has collapsed. Note also the dependence on the square of speed — taking that same bend at 21 m/s rather than 15 needs nearly twice the grip.

Banking solves the problem more elegantly by tilting the road so that a component of the normal force, rather than friction alone, points toward the centre. For a bend of radius r the ideal banking angle satisfies tanθ = v²/(rg), at which speed no friction at all is needed. Daytona International Speedway banks its turns at 31 degrees, letting cars corner far above any flat track's friction limit, while ordinary motorway slip roads use a few degrees for the same reason, mainly as a wet-weather margin.

The stubborn misconception is a centrifugal force flinging you outward. In the ground frame there is no outward force at all: your body's inertia is trying to continue in a straight line while the car curves out from beneath you, and the door pushes you inward. The outward sensation is real; the outward force is not. Within the rotating frame of the car a centrifugal term can be introduced as legitimate bookkeeping, but only because that frame is non-inertial.

sections.heading: The Two Faces of Friction: Why Things Stick, Then Slide
sections.body:
Friction has two distinct personalities, and knowing which is acting explains a great deal of everyday behaviour. Static friction resists the onset of relative motion between surfaces already in contact, and it is self-adjusting: it grows to match whatever applied force it opposes, cancelling it exactly, up to a maximum of μ_s times the normal force. Push a heavy dresser with 100 N and it does not move, because static friction supplies precisely 100 N back. Push with 200 N and it may still not move. Once the applied force exceeds that maximum, motion begins and friction drops abruptly to a lower, roughly constant kinetic value of μ_k times the normal force, with μ_k almost always the smaller coefficient. That drop is the physical reason a stuck drawer resists, resists, and then suddenly gives way and slides more easily than expected: the surplus of applied force over the now-smaller resistance accelerates it.

The same static-to-kinetic transition produces stick-slip motion — the squeal of chalk on a board, the creak of a door hinge, the note of a bowed violin string and the judder of worn brakes are all rapid cycles of sticking and slipping.

Typical coefficients vary enormously with the material pairing. Rubber on dry concrete runs about 0.6 to 0.9, which is why tyres grip. Wood on wood is about 0.2 to 0.5, steel on steel roughly 0.4 to 0.6 but falling to around 0.05 with oil between the surfaces, PTFE on steel about 0.04, and a waxed ski base on snow as low as 0.05 to 0.1, engineered deliberately small. Ice against a smooth sole can drop below 0.03, which accounts for most of why winter falls happen so suddenly: the static threshold that would normally warn you with a perceptible catch before slipping is barely there.

The most surprising result is that both coefficients depend only on the normal force and the material pairing, and not at all on the apparent area of contact. A brick dragged flat-side-down experiences the same friction as the same brick dragged on its narrow edge. The explanation lies at the microscopic scale. No surface is truly flat, and real contact happens only at scattered high points called asperities, whose combined true area is a tiny fraction of the apparent one. Pressing the same weight through a smaller apparent area raises the pressure proportionally and flattens those asperities until the true contact area comes out the same. Proportionality to load, rather than to area, follows.

Leonardo da Vinci recorded both results in his notebooks around 1493, but the manuscripts went unpublished for centuries and the field had to rediscover them from scratch: Guillaume Amontons published the same laws in 1699, and Charles-Augustin de Coulomb sharpened the static-kinetic distinction in 1785. These rules are empirical approximations rather than fundamental laws, and they break down for very clean surfaces, very high pressures, soft or tacky materials such as rubber at speed, and any situation where molecular adhesion dominates.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions That Even Careful Thinkers Fall Into
sections.body:
The most persistent misconception in mechanics is Aristotle's: that a constant force is needed to keep something moving, and that objects naturally run down to rest without one. It feels true because in ordinary experience friction and air resistance are always quietly present, decelerating anything not actively pushed. A rolling ball really does stop. But that stopping is the effect of an unbalanced force, not the absence of one, and the first law says the opposite — with no net force, motion continues unchanged indefinitely. Galileo's inclined-plane reasoning broke Aristotle's fourteen-century hold on the question: a ball rolled down one ramp climbs an opposing ramp back toward its original height, climbing ever closer as the surfaces are polished and whatever the second ramp's angle, so a second ramp laid flat implies motion without end.

A closely related myth is that heavier objects fall faster. In a vacuum every object near the Earth's surface accelerates downward at the same 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass, because the greater gravitational force on a heavier body is exactly offset by its proportionally greater inertia — the mass in W = mg and the mass in a = F/m cancel identically. What actually makes a feather fall more slowly than a hammer in air is drag, a separate force with no relation to gravity's pull, depending on cross-sectional area and shape rather than on mass. Commander David Scott released a hammer and a falcon feather together on the airless Moon during Apollo 15 in 1971, and they landed at the same instant.

Mass and weight are routinely conflated. Mass is an intrinsic quantity of matter measured in kilograms and unchanged anywhere in the universe; weight is the gravitational force on that mass, measured in newtons, and would be roughly a sixth as large on the Moon. Speed and velocity are confused just as often. Speed is a number; velocity is that number together with a direction, which is exactly why an object can hold perfectly constant speed while accelerating continuously, as anything moving in a circle does.

Two further traps deserve naming. The first is expecting a force in the direction of motion whenever something is moving. A ball thrown upward travels upward while the only force acting on it points down; between leaving the hand and returning to it there is no upward force at all, merely the velocity it was given. The second is treating action-reaction pairs as forces that cancel out. They act on different bodies and therefore cannot cancel.

Finally, many people expect an object released from a moving vehicle, or from a spinning turntable, to fly outward or drop straight down. It does neither. It carries on with exactly the velocity it had at the instant of release — forward for the vehicle, tangentially for the turntable — while gravity acts on it, which is simply the projectile case again. It is also why a passenger who drops something in a smoothly moving train watches it land at their feet.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
Nothing in mechanics needs a laboratory. Almost every quantitative result in the field can be reproduced with objects from a hardware shop, a hobby shop or a kitchen drawer, and it is worth understanding what each item is actually for, because the limiting factor in a home experiment is rarely the apparatus. It is measurement error, and each item below is chosen to keep one particular error small.

Timing is the weak link in nearly every mechanics measurement. Human reaction time, both starting and stopping a watch, runs around 0.2 s and varies from trial to trial, so timing a single event lasting one second carries an error of perhaps twenty per cent. The remedy is not a better stopwatch but a longer measurement: time twenty swings instead of one and the same reaction error is divided by twenty, falling to about one per cent. Any phone stopwatch is adequate once that trick is used.

A dense, compact weight matters because pendulum theory assumes all the mass sits at a single point. A large light object spreads its mass over too much space, leaving the effective length ambiguous. Something small and heavy makes the measured distance from pivot to centre of mass unambiguous, and its high density keeps air resistance negligible against its weight.

String should be thin and inextensible, because a stretchy cord changes length as the bob swings and quietly corrupts the very length that gets squared in the final calculation. A firm, rigid pivot matters for the same reason, since a springy hook adds motion of its own to the period.

A protractor matters because the standard pendulum formula assumes small angles, and knowing what fifteen degrees actually looks like is the only way to stay inside that approximation. Ramps and marbles let you study acceleration slowly enough to time by hand, since a slope reduces the acceleration to g times the sine of the angle. A spring or luggage scale reads force directly, letting a push be weighed rather than inferred.
ingredients: A stopwatch or any smartphone's built-in timer/stopwatch app (reaction-time error matters, so time multiple repetitions, not one)
A metric tape measure or meter stick, for distances and heights
A small, dense weight — a large steel nut, a fishing sinker, or a padlock — to serve as a pendulum bob
About 1.5 m of sturdy string or thin cord, plus a fixed point to hang it from (a doorframe hook, a coat hook, a sturdy branch)
A protractor or a printed protractor template, for measuring launch/release angles
Marbles or steel ball bearings, and a smooth ramp or length of rigid plastic/PVC channel to roll them down
A bathroom scale (for your own mass) and a kitchen scale (for smaller masses, in grams)
A spring scale or luggage scale (reads out in newtons or can be converted from kilograms) for measuring applied forces directly
Optional: a smartphone accelerometer app, which turns the phone itself into a basic force/acceleration sensor

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measure Gravitational Acceleration With a Pendulum
sections.body:
This is essentially Galileo's own method, refined, and one of the rare home experiments that yields a genuinely accurate physical constant. A simple pendulum swinging through a small arc has a period equal to 2π times the square root of L divided by g, where L is the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass of the bob. Rearranged, that gives g = 4π²L divided by T squared. Everything on the right is measurable with a tape and a stopwatch.

Two conditions carry the accuracy. The first is the small-angle requirement. The formula comes from approximating the sine of the angle by the angle itself, which is exact only in the limit of vanishing swing. At fifteen degrees the true period is longer than the formula predicts by roughly 0.4 per cent, which is acceptable; at forty-five degrees the error grows to nearly 4 per cent, which is not. The second is timing many swings rather than one, so that reaction-time error is divided across the count.

The comparison at three different lengths is the real payoff. Because the period depends on the square root of length, a pendulum four times longer swings only twice as slowly, and yet all three trials return the same value of g. That invariance is the entire point: g is a property of the Earth's gravitational field at your location, not of the apparatus, so a measurement reproducing it across changed conditions is evidence rather than coincidence. Genuine local variation does exist, from about 9.78 m/s² at the equator to 9.83 near the poles, but it sits well below the precision of any hand-timed experiment.
steps: Tie your weight to the string so that the distance from the pivot point to the CENTER of the weight is exactly 1.000 m — measure this carefully, since it's the value you'll square in the final calculation.
Hang the string from a fixed point (doorframe hook, sturdy branch) high enough that the weight can swing freely without hitting the floor, walls, or furniture.

Pull the weight to one side so the string makes no more than about 15° with the vertical, then release it from rest. (Small angles matter — the simple pendulum formula below is only accurate for small swings.)
Using your stopwatch, time exactly 20 complete back-and-forth swings, starting the timer the instant you release the weight and stopping it after the 20th full return to the starting side.
Divide your total time by 20 to get the period T (the time for one full swing).
Calculate g using g = 4π²L / T², where L = 1.000 m and T is in seconds.
Compare your result to 9.8 m/s². A well-run trial should land within a few percent; if it's far off, check that you counted swings correctly and that the angle stayed small.

Repeat the whole procedure with L = 0.5 m and L = 1.5 m. You should get essentially the same g both times — direct proof that the period depends on length, not on 'how much gravity there is,' a common misconception this experiment quietly demolishes.

guides.title: Energy, Work, Power & Simple Machines
guides.summary: What energy is and its forms, the exact definitions of work and power, the conservation of energy, efficiency, and how the six simple machines multiply force through mechanical advantage — with formulas, worked calculations, and practical examples from levers to pulleys.

sections.heading: Energy: the capacity to do work, and its forms
sections.body:
Energy is the capacity to do work or to cause change, and it is the most useful accounting quantity in all of physics, because although it takes many forms the total never alters. Its SI unit is the joule, defined so that one joule is one newton-metre — the work done pushing with a force of one newton through a distance of one metre — which in base units is one kilogram metre squared per second squared. That definition ties energy directly to force and distance, and it is worth holding onto, because every other energy unit turns out to be a repackaging of the same thing.

Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, possessed by anything with mass that is moving. Potential energy is stored energy of position or configuration, and it arrives in several flavours: gravitational, from height within a gravitational field; elastic, from a deformed spring or stretched rubber; chemical, held in the arrangement of electrons within molecular bonds; and nuclear, held in the binding of the atomic nucleus. Thermal energy is not a separate kind of thing at all but simply the kinetic energy of vast numbers of randomly moving particles, which is precisely why temperature and molecular speed track one another. Electrical energy, radiant energy carried by light, and sound energy carried as pressure waves complete the everyday list.

The unifying insight is that all of these are one currency in different denominations, and any of them can in principle be converted into any other. A hydroelectric dam is a chain of such conversions: water held high behind the wall carries gravitational potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy as it falls down the penstock, which becomes rotational energy in the turbine, which becomes electrical energy in the generator, which becomes light, heat and motion inside a house many kilometres away. At every stage some energy leaks off as heat and sound, but none of it is destroyed.

Several other energy units survive for historical reasons and are worth being able to convert. The calorie, originally the heat needed to raise one gram of water by one degree Celsius, equals 4.184 joules; the dietary Calorie printed on food packaging is actually a kilocalorie, or 4,184 joules. The kilowatt-hour, the unit on an electricity bill, is a power multiplied by a time and equals 3.6 million joules. The electronvolt, used in atomic and particle physics because joules are absurdly large at that scale, is 1.602 times ten to the minus nineteen joules. The British thermal unit, still common in heating and air conditioning, is about 1,055 joules. Recognising that all of these measure the same physical quantity is what allows a food label, a fuel tank and a power bill to be compared directly.

sections.heading: Work: force acting through a distance
sections.body:
In everyday speech, work means effort. In physics it means something narrower and far more precise: work is done only when a force moves its point of application through a distance, and only the component of that force lying along the displacement counts at all. The defining equation is W = F·d·cos θ, where W is work in joules, F is force in newtons, d is displacement in metres, and θ is the angle between the direction of the force and the direction of motion.

The cosine factor is where most of the physical content lives. When force and motion point the same way, θ is zero, cos θ is one, and the expression collapses to the familiar W = F·d. When the force is perpendicular to the motion, θ is ninety degrees, cos θ is zero, and no work is done whatever — which produces the classic and initially infuriating result that carrying a heavy suitcase horizontally at constant height does zero work on the suitcase. The supporting force points upward, the motion is sideways, and the two are perpendicular. You still tire, because muscle fibres cycle chemically to maintain tension even when they do not shorten, but that energy is spent inside your body and never transfers to the case. Lift the same case one metre, however, and you genuinely do work against gravity equal to its weight multiplied by that metre. When a force opposes motion, θ exceeds ninety degrees, the cosine goes negative, and so does the work: friction and braking remove energy from a moving object rather than adding it.

Work is a scalar rather than a vector — it has magnitude but no direction — so contributions simply add algebraically, which is exactly what makes energy bookkeeping easier than tracking forces. Two further conventions matter in practice. Work is counted positive when a force adds energy to an object and negative when it removes energy, so a rope hauling a crate up a slope does positive work while friction along that same slope simultaneously does negative work, and the net work on the crate is simply the sum of the two.

Consider a worked example. You push a lawnmower with a force of 100 newtons directed along a handle angled 30 degrees below horizontal, moving it 20 metres across the lawn. The work done on the mower is 100 × 20 × cos 30°, and since cos 30° is 0.866, that comes to 1,732 joules. The remaining component of your push, 100 × sin 30° = 50 newtons pointing downward, does no work at all, because the mower never moves downward. It merely presses the mower harder into the turf, which incidentally increases the friction you then have to overcome. Pushing along a shallower handle angle would deliver more of the same effort as useful work — one of the small practical payoffs of taking the cosine seriously rather than treating it as decoration.

sections.heading: Kinetic and potential energy formulas
sections.body:
Two equations carry most of the everyday weight in mechanics, and both reward being understood structurally rather than merely memorised.

Kinetic energy, the energy an object possesses by virtue of moving, is KE = ½mv², with m the mass in kilograms, v the speed in metres per second, and the result in joules. The crucial structural feature is that speed appears squared while mass appears only to the first power. Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy; doubling the speed quadruples it. This is not a mathematical curiosity but the reason road-safety arithmetic works out as it does. A car travelling at 60 kilometres per hour carries four times the kinetic energy of the same car at 30, and since braking dissipates that energy over distance at a roughly constant friction force, the braking distance is also roughly four times longer. Triple the speed and the energy is nine times greater. The same squared relationship explains why a small hailstone falling fast can shatter a window that a much heavier ball rolled gently against it cannot.

Gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface is PE = mgh, where g is the gravitational field strength of about 9.8 metres per second squared and h is the height above whatever reference level you choose. That choice is arbitrary and does not matter, because only changes in potential energy have physical consequences — which is why it is perfectly legitimate to call the floor zero in one problem and the tabletop zero in the next. Strictly, g is not a universal constant either: it is about 9.83 metres per second squared at the poles and 9.78 at the equator, because the Earth bulges and rotates, and it falls slowly with altitude. Within a few kilometres of the surface, 9.8 is accurate to well under one per cent and the distinction rarely matters.

A worked example shows the two equations meeting. A 2-kilogram rock is held 5 metres above the ground, giving it a potential energy of 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 joules relative to the ground. Released, it converts that potential energy steadily into kinetic energy as it falls. Just before impact, ignoring air resistance, all 98 joules are kinetic, so ½ × 2 × v² = 98, giving v² = 98 and v ≈ 9.9 metres per second. That agrees exactly with the kinematic result v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 5), as it must, since the two calculations describe identical physics through different bookkeeping. Notice that mass cancels entirely from the second form: a 2-kilogram rock and a 20-kilogram rock dropped from the same height strike the ground at the same speed. Galileo's observation falls straight out of energy conservation, without any experiment being needed to establish it.

sections.heading: Conservation of energy and the work-energy theorem
sections.body:
The Law of Conservation of Energy is among the deepest statements in science: energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only converted between forms, so the total energy of an isolated system stays constant. This is not a rule assembled from a handful of experiments. Through Noether's theorem it follows from the fact that the laws of physics do not change from one moment to the next — a symmetry of time itself.

For a mechanical system without friction, the statement takes a directly usable form: the sum of kinetic and potential energy is identical at every point of the motion, so KE_initial + PE_initial = KE_final + PE_final. A frictionless roller coaster is the standard illustration. At the crest of the first hill the car is high and slow, holding nearly all its energy as potential; at the bottom it is low and fast, holding nearly all of it as kinetic; at every point between, the two add to the same total. This is why no later hill can be built taller than the first, and why calculating the car's speed anywhere on the track requires no knowledge whatever of the shape of the rails in between — only the difference in height.

The work-energy theorem connects force to speed directly: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, W_net = ΔKE = ½mv_final² − ½mv_initial². This is frequently the fastest route to an answer, because it sidesteps time entirely. Asked how far a 1,200-kilogram car travelling at 20 metres per second goes while braking under a constant 6,000-newton friction force, the theorem answers immediately: kinetic energy of ½ × 1,200 × 400 = 240,000 joules must be removed by work of 6,000 × d, so d = 40 metres.

Where friction or air drag is present, mechanical energy is not conserved as mechanical energy — but it is not lost either. It converts into thermal energy, meaning the disordered kinetic energy of countless molecules in the brake discs, the tyres and the surrounding air. The total is unchanged; only its orderliness declines, which is the province of the second law of thermodynamics rather than the first. A pendulum makes the point cleanly. Released from a height of 0.20 metres, the bob reaches a maximum speed at the bottom of √(2 × 9.8 × 0.20) ≈ 1.98 metres per second. If friction at the pivot and drag through the air remove ten per cent of its energy each swing, it rises to only 0.18 metres on the far side. The missing energy, mg × 0.02 joules, has warmed the pivot and the air by an amount far too small to feel and yet exactly accounted for.

sections.heading: Power: the rate of doing work
sections.body:
Power measures how quickly work is done or energy transferred, and it is usually the quantity people mean when they loosely call something powerful. Work says how much; power says how fast. A frail person and a strong one carrying the same load up the same staircase do exactly the same work against gravity, because work depends only on weight and height. The strong one who arrives in half the time has delivered twice the power.

The definition is P = W/t, equivalently P = E/t, with power in watts, where one watt is one joule per second. A convenient alternative applies when a steady force pushes something along at steady speed: work is force times distance and speed is distance over time, so power equals force times velocity, P = F·v. That form explains why a vehicle's top speed is set by power rather than by force. Aerodynamic drag grows roughly with the square of speed, so the power needed to overcome it grows roughly with the cube, and each further increment of speed costs disproportionately more.

Benchmarks make the unit meaningful. One horsepower, defined by James Watt from the sustained output of a working draught horse, is 746 watts. A person walking briskly upstairs produces roughly 200 watts of mechanical output. A trained sprinter briefly peaks somewhere near 1,000 to 2,000 watts but can sustain only a fraction of it; a fit cyclist holds 250 to 400 watts for an hour, while an ordinary person averages closer to 100 watts across a working day. A family car engine delivers 75 to 150 kilowatts, the mechanical equivalent of several hundred people. One caution about vocabulary belongs here: a kilowatt is a rate, while a kilowatt-hour is a quantity, and confusing the two is as wrong as reporting the length of a journey in kilometres per hour.

A worked example ties the definitions together. A 60-kilogram person climbs a flight of stairs 3 metres high in 4 seconds.
