The work done against gravity is mgh = 60 × 9.8 × 3 = 1,764 joules, so the power is 1,764 ÷ 4 = 441 watts, about 0.59 horsepower. That figure counts only useful mechanical output; the metabolic cost is roughly four to five times greater, because muscle converts fuel to work at only twenty to twenty-five per cent efficiency.

Electricity billing multiplies power by time rather than dividing by it. A 2,000-watt heater run for three hours consumes 2 kilowatts × 3 hours = 6 kilowatt-hours, and at fifteen cents per kilowatt-hour that costs ninety cents. The same arithmetic applied to every appliance in a house is the whole of domestic energy budgeting, and it explains why a heater left on for an afternoon dwarfs the contribution of a phone charger left plugged in all year.

sections.heading: The six simple machines and mechanical advantage
sections.body:
A machine cannot create energy. What it can do is trade force against distance, letting a small force applied along a long path accomplish what would otherwise demand a large force over a short one. The ratio of the load moved to the effort applied is the mechanical advantage, MA = load ÷ effort. A machine with a mechanical advantage of four lets you lift a weight with a quarter of the force, at the price of pulling four times as far, because the energy going in must at least equal the energy coming out.

The lever is the archetype: a rigid bar turning about a fulcrum, with an ideal mechanical advantage equal to the length of the effort arm divided by the length of the load arm. A crowbar gripped two metres from the pivot, prying a load ten centimetres from it, multiplies force twenty-fold. Levers are classified by the arrangement of fulcrum, effort and load: a seesaw puts the fulcrum in the middle, a wheelbarrow puts the load in the middle, and the human forearm puts the effort in the middle, which gives it a mechanical advantage below one. That sounds like a design fault until you notice the trade runs the other way — the biceps shortens by a few centimetres while the hand sweeps through tens of centimetres, buying speed and range at the cost of force.

A wheel and axle is a rotating lever, with mechanical advantage equal to the wheel radius divided by the axle radius; doorknobs, steering wheels, screwdrivers and hand winches all exploit it. A pulley system has a mechanical advantage roughly equal to the number of rope segments actually supporting the load, so a single fixed pulley gives an advantage of one and merely redirects the effort somewhere more convenient, while a block and tackle with four supporting strands gives four. An inclined plane has mechanical advantage equal to its length divided by its height, so rolling a barrel up a five-metre ramp to a height of one metre needs one-fifth the force of lifting it, over five times the distance. A wedge is an inclined plane driven point-first, converting a blow along its length into a much larger force pushing the material apart sideways — axes, knives, chisels and nails all work this way. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder, and because a full turn advances it only by the small pitch between threads, its mechanical advantage is very large, which is why a car jack or a bench vice generates enormous force from a modest twist of the hand.

Every complicated machine is assembled from these six building blocks in combination.

sections.heading: Efficiency, friction, and real machines
sections.body:
No real machine is ideal, because some of the energy put in always ends up somewhere unintended — heating rubbing surfaces, deforming components, stirring air, making noise. Efficiency measures what fraction arrives where you wanted it: useful energy output divided by total energy input, conventionally written as a percentage. For a force-multiplying machine there is an equivalent form, efficiency equals actual mechanical advantage divided by ideal mechanical advantage, which is convenient because both quantities can be measured with a spring balance rather than a calorimeter.

The numbers vary enormously by machine type, and the pattern is instructive. A well-lubricated pulley block might reach ninety per cent, while a rusted one struggles past sixty. A bicycle drivetrain is among the most efficient machines ever built, at roughly ninety-five per cent. A good electric motor commonly exceeds ninety per cent. By contrast, a petrol internal-combustion engine converts only about twenty-five to thirty per cent of its fuel's chemical energy into useful shaft work, with most of the remainder leaving as exhaust heat and through the radiator — and that is not merely poor engineering but partly a hard thermodynamic ceiling, since any heat engine is limited by the temperatures between which it operates. Incandescent light bulbs were about five per cent efficient as sources of light, which is precisely why they were legislated out of existence.

A worked example makes the arithmetic concrete. A ramp has an ideal mechanical advantage of five, and a 500-newton barrel is to be pushed up it. In an ideal world 100 newtons would suffice, but friction means the barrel actually needs 125 newtons. The actual mechanical advantage is therefore 500 ÷ 125 = 4, and the efficiency is 4 ÷ 5, or 80 per cent. The missing fifth of the work has warmed the ramp and the barrel by a small but entirely real amount.

Several practical consequences follow. Lubrication with oil, grease or rolling-element bearings raises efficiency by cutting friction, but friction is not simply an enemy: brakes, tyres, nails, knots and walking itself all depend on it, and a frictionless world would be unusable. The force-for-distance trade is unavoidable, which is why a high-advantage car jack demands many turns of the handle for a few centimetres of lift, and why a low-gear bicycle climbs a hill easily but slowly. Every machine carries a rated working load, and exceeding it risks sudden rather than gradual failure, particularly in cables and slings where there is no visible warning first. And the first law forbids perpetual motion outright: any device claimed to deliver more energy than it consumes is either mismeasured or fraudulent, with no third possibility worth entertaining. Such claims invariably rest on an unmeasured input or an unmeasured output, and identifying which one is the whole of the debunking.

sections.heading: Elastic Potential Energy and Hooke's Law: The Physics of Springs
sections.body:
A stretched or compressed spring stores energy just as surely as a lifted weight does, except that the energy resides in the strained arrangement of atoms within the material rather than in height above the ground. For an ideal spring the restoring force is proportional to displacement from the natural length: F = −kx, where k is the spring constant in newtons per metre, and the minus sign records that the force always points back toward equilibrium. This is Hooke's Law. It is an approximation that holds well up to a material's elastic limit and then fails — beyond that point the spring deforms permanently and never recovers its original length, which is exactly what has happened to any spring that has gone slack.

The stored elastic potential energy is PE = ½kx². The factor of one half appears because the force is not constant during the stretch: it begins at zero and rises linearly to kx, so the average force across the stretch is half the maximum, and work is average force times distance. Graphically, the stored energy is the triangular area beneath the force-versus-displacement line, in the same way that the area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement. Note the squared term: stretching a spring twice as far stores four times the energy, which is why the last centimetre of draw on a bow contributes far more than the first. Real springs also carry a maximum working deflection specified by the manufacturer, and repeated cycling near that limit produces fatigue failure long before any single overload would.

Robert Hooke established the relationship around 1660, but in the fiercely competitive scientific culture of the early Royal Society he published it in 1676 only as a scrambled Latin anagram, ceiiinosssttuv, staking his priority without revealing anything useful to rivals. He disclosed the solution in 1678: ut tensio, sic vis — as the extension, so the force.

A worked example with real stakes. A car's front suspension spring has a stiffness of roughly 25,000 newtons per metre. Striking a pothole compresses it by 4 centimetres, or 0.04 metres, storing ½ × 25,000 × 0.04² = 20 joules. That energy has to go somewhere. In a working car the shock absorber converts it into heat by forcing oil through small orifices, dissipating it over the following second so the body settles once and stays settled. When shock absorbers wear out, nothing dissipates it, so the spring simply hands the energy back to the body, which bounces repeatedly after every bump — the same 20 joules sloshing between spring and mass, with the tyre briefly unloading at the top of each bounce and taking the braking and steering grip with it. That is why worn dampers are a safety fault rather than a comfort complaint.

sections.heading: Human Energy: Metabolism, Food Calories, and the Body as an Engine
sections.body:
The human body is, in a strictly thermodynamic sense, an engine that burns chemical fuel to produce mechanical work, and food Calories are ordinary energy units wearing familiar clothes. The dietary Calorie, written with a capital C, is a kilocalorie and equals 4,184 joules. Muscle, however, is a mediocre converter: only about twenty to twenty-five per cent of the chemical energy released during exertion emerges as useful mechanical work, while the remaining three-quarters appears as heat. That is not a defect to be trained away — it is why hard exercise makes you hot within minutes, and why sweating exists at all, since a working body must shed roughly three watts of waste heat for every watt of useful output.

That efficiency figure produces a genuinely startling comparison. A typical jam doughnut holds around 250 kilocalories, which is 250 × 4,184 ≈ 1,046,000 joules of chemical energy. If a 70-kilogram person converted that into climbing at twenty-five per cent muscular efficiency, the usable mechanical work would be about 261,500 joules. Since climbing work is W = mgh, the achievable height is h = W ÷ (mg) = 261,500 ÷ (70 × 9.8) ≈ 381 metres. The number is not rounded for effect: it lands almost exactly on the 381-metre roof height of the Empire State Building, excluding the antenna mast that brings the total to 443 metres. One doughnut, metabolised with perfect focus, is roughly enough chemical energy to climb New York's most famous skyscraper.

The same ceiling explains why exercising food off is so much harder than eating it. A brisk hour-long walk expends perhaps 200 to 300 kilocalories of total metabolic cost, a modest fraction of a single meal, because most of that chemical energy never becomes motion at all. It is worth being careful with the accounting here, since the two figures are routinely conflated: 200 to 300 kilocalories is metabolic expenditure, and the mechanical work actually performed is only about a quarter of it.

Basal metabolism dominates the daily budget for most people. A resting adult burns roughly 1,400 to 1,800 kilocalories per day simply maintaining body temperature, ion gradients across cell membranes, protein turnover and circulation, which corresponds to a continuous output near 70 to 90 watts — comparable to an old incandescent bulb. A crowded room genuinely warms up for exactly this reason, and lecture theatres are ventilated on that assumption. Deliberate exercise typically adds only a few hundred kilocalories on top of that baseline, which is why diet dominates energy-balance arithmetic, and why the body is best understood as a furnace that idles expensively rather than an engine that runs only when working. One further caution: muscular efficiency varies by activity, reaching its highest values for cycling at a steady cadence and falling considerably for tasks such as digging, where much of the effort goes into stabilising the body rather than moving the load.

sections.heading: Rotational Work, Torque, and Spinning Energy
sections.body:
Every statement about force, work and energy has a rotational counterpart, and the translation is almost mechanical: force becomes torque, mass becomes moment of inertia, and linear velocity becomes angular velocity. Torque, τ = r·F·sin θ, measures how effectively a force twists something about a pivot, depending on the size of the force, the distance from the pivot, and the angle at which it is applied. This is why a longer wrench loosens a stuck bolt more easily. The same 150-newton pull applied at 0.25 metres produces 37.5 newton-metres of torque, against only 15 newton-metres from a stubby 0.10-metre handle — two and a half times the twisting effect from identical muscular effort. It is also why passenger-car wheel nuts are specified at roughly 100 to 140 newton-metres, and why mechanics reach that figure with a long torque wrench rather than heroically.

Rotational kinetic energy is KE = ½Iω², where ω is angular velocity in radians per second and I is the moment of inertia, the rotational analogue of mass. Unlike mass, I depends not only on how much material there is but on where that material sits relative to the axis: a solid disc of mass m and radius r has I = ½mr², whereas a hoop with all its mass out at the rim has I = mr², twice as much. Moving mass outward raises I sharply, because each element contributes in proportion to the square of its distance from the axis. This is the entire explanation for a spinning skater accelerating as the arms are pulled in — angular momentum Iω is conserved, so reducing I must increase ω. The same principle sets a diver's somersault rate, and explains why a long pole helps a tightrope walker: it raises the moment of inertia about the wire, so any given toppling torque produces a slower angular acceleration, buying time to correct.

Flywheel energy storage follows directly from those two facts. Take a solid steel disc of 50 kilograms and 0.3 metres radius, spun to 3,000 revolutions per minute. Converting, ω = 3,000 × 2π ÷ 60 ≈ 314 radians per second, and I = ½ × 50 × 0.3² = 2.25 kilogram metres squared. The stored energy is ½ × 2.25 × 314² ≈ 111,000 joules — over a hundred kilojoules held purely as spin, available on demand. Because energy scales with the square of angular velocity, doubling the rotation rate quadruples the storage, which is why practical flywheels are spun as fast as material strength allows rather than simply built heavier.

Real transit systems and data-centre backup supplies use exactly this trick, spinning heavy rotors up during braking or surplus generation and drawing the energy back out later, with no chemical battery involved and none of the capacity loss that repeated charge cycles inflict on one.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
Everything in this subject can be measured with equipment already present in most homes, and that is not a compromise — it is the point. Energy, work and power are defined entirely in terms of mass, distance and time, so a scale, a tape measure and a clock are in principle sufficient to measure any of them. There is no hidden instrument that professionals use instead.

A few practical notes make the measurements trustworthy. Mass must be expressed in kilograms for the formulas to yield joules and watts directly. A scale reading in pounds needs dividing by 2.205; getting this wrong is the commonest source of an answer wrong by a factor of two.

Height must be measured vertically rather than along the slope of the stairs. A staircase's diagonal length is substantially greater than its vertical rise, and using it inflates the result by thirty per cent or more. Measuring one riser precisely — typically between 0.15 and 0.19 metres in domestic construction — and multiplying by the number of steps is usually more accurate than trying to hold a tape vertically down a stairwell, because a tape that sags or leans always reads long.

Timing is the weakest link in any hand-run experiment. Human reaction time is around 0.2 seconds at each end, so a four-second climb carries roughly ten per cent uncertainty on that basis alone. A second person on the stopwatch, and three runs averaged rather than one, is worth the trouble. Report the answer to two significant figures rather than the eight the calculator offers: claiming 441.23 watts from a hand-timed measurement is false precision.

For the spring experiment, known masses matter far more than an expensive spring. Water is the most convenient standard available, since one litre has a mass of almost exactly one kilogram — that equivalence is where the original metric system began — so a marked bottle is effectively a calibrated weight. Hang the spring from something genuinely rigid, since a flexing support adds its own extension to every reading, tape a ruler alongside it, and measure from the same fixed point each time. Reading from the coil once and the hook next time introduces an offset that quietly spoils the straight line you are looking for.
ingredients: A bathroom scale, to measure your own body mass
A tape measure or meter stick, to measure the vertical rise of a staircase
A stopwatch or a smartphone timer app
A set of stairs (at home, an apartment stairwell, or any public staircase you have safe access to)
A spring or a length of coil-spring material (an old ballpoint-pen spring, a slinky, or a small hardware-store extension spring) if you want to also verify Hooke's law
A kitchen scale that reads in grams, plus a set of known weights (bags of sugar/flour of labeled weight, or bottled water — 1 liter of water is almost exactly 1 kg) for the spring experiment
A ruler taped alongside the hanging spring, to read extension distances

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measure Your Own Horsepower on a Staircase
sections.body:
This is the classic power laboratory, and it works because the quantity measured is genuinely your own: the mechanical output of your legs, in watts, from nothing but a scale, a tape measure and a stopwatch.

The physics is contained in a single substitution. The work done climbing is work done against gravity, mgh — your weight multiplied by the vertical height gained — and power is that work divided by the time taken, so P = mgh/t. Nothing about the staircase's shape, its number of steps, or the path across each landing enters the calculation. Only the vertical rise matters, because gravity is a conservative force and horizontal movement does no work against it.

Two caveats keep the result honest. First, this measures mechanical output alone. Metabolic expenditure is four to five times larger, because muscle converts chemical energy into work at only twenty to twenty-five per cent efficiency, so a 441-watt climb costs the body closer to 1,800 watts of fuel, most of it emerging as heat. Second, a burst up one flight is not sustainable output. Peak power across a few seconds draws on stored phosphocreatine and anaerobic glycolysis, neither lasting more than tens of seconds. That is why half a horsepower for four seconds sits comfortably alongside roughly 0.13 horsepower averaged over an hour, with no contradiction.

The final comparison is the one worth doing carefully, because it isolates the distinction this whole topic rests on. Climbing the same stairs slowly and then quickly involves identical work — the same mass raised the same height — but markedly different power. Work is the total; power is the rate.
steps: Weigh yourself on a bathroom scale in kilograms (if it reads in pounds, divide by 2.205) to get your mass m.

Measure the total vertical rise of your staircase: either measure the height of one riser (typically 0.15–0.19 m) with a tape measure and multiply by the number of steps, or measure the total floor-to-floor height directly with a tape measure alongside the stairwell.

Warm up briefly, then have someone start a stopwatch the instant you begin, and stop it the instant you reach the top — climb at a hard but safe pace, using the handrail, without leaping steps dangerously.
Record your climb time t in seconds.
Calculate the mechanical power output: P = mgh / t, where g = 9.8 m/s².

Convert to horsepower by dividing by 746 (1 hp = 746 W) to see what fraction of a 'horsepower' your legs briefly produced — most people land somewhere between 0.3 and 0.6 hp in a hard sprint up a flight of stairs, a number completely out of reach for sustained effort (your body can only average roughly 100 W, about 0.13 hp, over an hour of continuous work).

Try it again at a slow, comfortable walking pace up the same stairs and recalculate — you did exactly the same amount of WORK both times (same mgh), but a dramatically different amount of POWER, since power is work divided by time. This is the clearest possible demonstration that work and power are not the same quantity.

guides.title: Electricity & Magnetism
guides.summary: Electric charge, current, voltage and resistance; Ohm's law and how to calculate them; series versus parallel circuits; electrical power and safety; magnetism, electromagnets, and how motors and generators turn electricity and motion into one another — with formulas, worked circuits, and life-saving safety rules.

sections.heading: Electric charge: the source of all electrical phenomena
sections.body:
Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter, like mass: it is not built out of anything more basic, cannot be created or destroyed, and can only be moved from place to place. Charge comes in two kinds, positive and negative, named by Benjamin Franklin in a convention that runs backwards for metals yet is still used universally. Each proton in an atomic nucleus carries one unit of positive charge; each electron in the surrounding cloud carries one unit of negative. The governing rule is that like charges repel and opposite charges attract. The SI unit of charge is the coulomb, symbol C. One electron carries −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so a single coulomb is the combined charge of roughly 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. That number is the first clue that ordinary matter must be almost perfectly balanced.

Neutrality is aggressively enforced. Compare the two forces acting between a pair of electrons: the electric repulsion is about 10⁴² times stronger than their gravitational attraction. Gravity dominates the universe at large scales only because charge cancels so thoroughly and mass does not. In practice you can separate only a vanishingly small fraction, which is why static electricity, dramatic as it feels, involves nanocoulombs to microcoulombs at most.

Static charging happens by contact and separation. When two dissimilar materials touch and part, electrons transfer from the one that holds them loosely to the one that holds them tightly, a ranking captured by the triboelectric series: human hair, wool and glass give electrons up readily, while rubber, PTFE and polyester take them. Rub a balloon on hair and the balloon leaves negative and the hair positive, so the strands repel one another and stand up while both are drawn toward the balloon. It is always electrons that move; protons are locked inside nuclei and never travel in everyday physics. Humidity matters: a thin film of adsorbed water on surfaces conducts the charge away, which is why static shocks plague dry winter air and largely vanish above about sixty per cent relative humidity.

Charge is conserved absolutely. It flows freely through conductors such as copper, aluminium and salt water, where outer electrons are shared across the whole material, and barely at all through insulators such as dry air, glass, rubber and most plastics, where each electron stays bound to its own atom. Grounding simply provides a conductive path to the enormous charge reservoir of the Earth. The practical consequence is electrostatic discharge damage: a person walking across carpet can reach 10,000 to 15,000 volts, yet you only feel a spark above about 3,000 volts, and many semiconductor gates fail permanently at 100 volts or less. A chip can therefore be destroyed by a shock you never noticed, which is why they are handled with wrist straps on anti-static mats. Lightning is the same physics at extreme scale: charge separation inside a storm cloud builds until the field exceeds the roughly 3 MV per metre that dry air can withstand, and a channel of ionised air carries tens of thousands of amperes to ground.

sections.heading: Current, voltage and resistance defined
sections.body:
Three quantities describe the behaviour of any electrical circuit, and keeping them straight is the single most useful skill in the subject. A plumbing picture helps as a first approximation: voltage resembles water pressure, current resembles flow rate, and resistance resembles the narrowness of the pipe. The analogy has real limits, but it correctly captures which quantity causes which and is worth holding onto.

Current, symbol I, is the rate at which electric charge passes a point, written I = Q/t, and measured in amperes. One ampere is one coulomb per second, roughly 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons streaming past each second. Current flows through a component, so an ammeter must be inserted into the circuit in series, with the current physically routed through the meter. Conventional current is defined as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative, the direction positive charge would move, even though in a metal wire the actual carriers are electrons drifting the opposite way. This is a historical accident from before the electron was discovered, but the two descriptions are mathematically equivalent.

Voltage, symbol V, also called potential difference or electromotive force, is the energy delivered to each coulomb of charge, measured in volts. One volt is one joule per coulomb. The crucial point is that voltage is a difference between two points, so it is always measured across a component, with the voltmeter's two probes touching either side. Asking for the voltage at a single point is meaningless without a stated reference, which is what a circuit's ground node provides. A 1.5 V cell gives every coulomb 1.5 joules as it passes through.

Resistance, symbol R, is the opposition a material offers to charge flow, measured in ohms. It is not arbitrary but follows from geometry and material: R = ρL/A, where ρ is resistivity, L is length and A is cross-sectional area. Copper's resistivity is 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, so 10 m of 1.5 mm² household wire has about 0.11 Ω of resistance, negligible for a lamp but not for a kettle. Resistance also rises with temperature in metals, by roughly 0.4 per cent per degree Celsius for copper, which is why a tungsten filament's cold resistance can be a fifteenth of its hot value and why bulbs almost always fail at switch-on.

One genuinely surprising fact: the electrons themselves crawl. In a typical household wire carrying a few amperes, the drift velocity is on the order of 0.1 millimetres per second, so an individual electron takes hours to travel a metre. Yet the lamp lights instantly, because the electric field that pushes the electrons propagates along the wire at a substantial fraction of light speed, and the wire is already full of mobile charge. Everything shoves at once, like water in an already full pipe. The analogy's main failure is that water can leak out of a broken pipe whereas current requires a complete loop; a practical corollary is that clipping a multimeter set to current mode across a battery creates a near short circuit and blows the meter's internal fuse, a mistake almost every beginner makes once.

sections.heading: Ohm's Law and worked circuit calculations
sections.body:
Ohm's Law is the central working relationship of circuit analysis, published by Georg Ohm in 1827 after careful measurements that were initially dismissed by his contemporaries. It states that the voltage across a conductor equals the current through it times its resistance: V = I·R, with V in volts, I in amperes and R in ohms. Because it is a simple product, it rearranges two ways used constantly in practice. To find the current a source drives through a known resistance, use I = V/R. To find an unknown resistance from meter readings, use R = V/I. Committing all three forms to memory takes minutes and pays back permanently.

A first worked example is the most common real task in hobby electronics: protecting a light-emitting diode. Suppose you have a 9 V battery and an LED that drops about 2 V across itself and is rated for 20 milliamperes, which is 0.020 amperes. The LED cannot limit its own current, so a series resistor must absorb the remaining voltage. That leftover is 7 V, and the required resistance is R = 7/0.020 = 350 Ω. Standard resistors come in fixed values, so you would fit the next value up, 360 or 390 Ω, erring toward slightly less current rather than more. Always check the resistor's own dissipation too: P = I²R gives about 0.14 W, comfortably inside a common quarter-watt part. Fitting no resistor at all is the classic beginner error, and the LED typically survives a second or less.

A second example runs the other direction. A domestic heater draws 10 amperes from a 240 V supply, so its resistance is R equals 240 divided by 10, which is 24 ohms. That figure is the hot, operating resistance. Measure the same element cold with a meter and you may read appreciably less, because metallic resistance climbs with temperature. The same effect explains inrush current: a tungsten filament lamp can momentarily draw ten to fifteen times its steady current in the first few milliseconds after switch-on, which is why filament lamps overwhelmingly fail at the moment you flick the switch rather than during steady burning.

The honest caveat is that Ohm's Law is not a universal law of nature in the way conservation of charge is. It is a statement that certain materials, called ohmic, have a resistance that stays constant over the range of interest. Metals at steady temperature obey it well. Many everyday components do not. A silicon diode's current rises roughly exponentially with voltage, conducting almost nothing below about 0.6 V and then very steeply above it. A thermistor's resistance is deliberately designed to swing with temperature. A filament lamp is non-ohmic precisely because it gets hot. For these, the ratio V divided by I is still a meaningful resistance at one particular operating point, but it changes as conditions change, so the correct approach is to work from the component's datasheet curve rather than assume a single number holds everywhere.

sections.heading: Series and parallel circuits
sections.body:
There are exactly two fundamental ways to connect components, and almost every circuit you will meet is a combination of them. Telling them apart is the difference between a design that works and one that burns.

In a series connection the components sit in a single loop, one after another, so charge must pass through every one in turn. Three consequences follow directly. The same current flows through all of them, because there is nowhere else for it to go. The individual voltages add up to the supply voltage, since the energy each coulomb received from the source is spent piece by piece along the way. And the resistances add: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ and so on. The total is always larger than any single resistor. The classic weakness is that a single failure breaks the whole loop, which is why old series-wired Christmas lights all went dark when one bulb blew, and why finding the culprit meant testing every bulb.

In a parallel connection the components sit on separate branches between the same two junctions, so charge arriving at the first junction chooses a path. Again three consequences follow. The same voltage appears across every branch, because each branch spans the identical pair of points. The branch currents add to give the total drawn from the source. And the resistances combine reciprocally: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ and so on, so the total is always smaller than the smallest branch. Adding a parallel path is adding another lane to a road; more traffic gets through for the same pressure.

Work a concrete pair. Take R₁ = 6 Ω and R₂ = 3 Ω. In series the total is 6 + 3 = 9 Ω, and on a 9 V supply the current is 1 A, with 6 V dropped across the larger resistor and 3 V across the smaller. In parallel, 1/R_total = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6, so R_total = 2 Ω, and the same 9 V supply now delivers 4.5 A, split as 1.5 A through the 6 Ω branch and 3 A through the 3 Ω branch. Notice the total, 2 Ω, is below the smaller of the two resistors, which consistently surprises people the first time they meet it. For two resistors specifically the shortcut R_total = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) saves arithmetic, and n identical resistors in parallel give simply R/n.

Domestic wiring is parallel for good reasons. Every socket then sees the full 120 V or 230 V regardless of what else is plugged in, and switching one appliance off does not interrupt the others. The hazard is the flip side of the same maths: every extra appliance lowers the total resistance and raises the total current in the shared supply cable feeding the circuit. Plug enough heaters into one 13 A ring and the cable, not the appliances, overheats, which is precisely what a circuit breaker exists to prevent. This is also why daisy-chained extension leads are dangerous even though each individual appliance is fine on its own.

sections.heading: Electrical power and energy cost
sections.body:
Power is the rate at which energy is converted from one form to another, and in a circuit it is the rate at which electrical energy becomes heat, light or motion. The primary expression is P = V·I, where P is power in watts, V is voltage in volts and I is current in amperes. The derivation is worth seeing: a volt is a joule per coulomb and an ampere is a coulomb per second, so multiplying them gives joules per second, which is the definition of a watt. Substituting Ohm's Law produces two equivalent forms that are often more convenient: P = I²R when you know the current and resistance, and P = V²/R when you know the voltage and resistance. All three describe the same physical quantity; use whichever matches the numbers you actually have.

A worked example makes the relationships concrete. A 60 W incandescent lamp on a 120 V supply draws I = P/V = 60/120 = 0.5 A and has an operating resistance of R = V²/P = 120²/60 = 240 Ω. On a 230 V supply, a 60 W lamp instead draws only 0.26 A and must have a resistance of about 880 Ω, which is why lamps and appliances are not interchangeable between regions and why plugging a 120 V device into 230 V roughly quadruples its power and destroys it almost immediately.

Energy is power multiplied by time, and it is energy, not power, that appears on a bill. Utilities meter in kilowatt-hours: one kilowatt drawn for one hour, which is 3.6 million joules. A 1,500 W space heater run five hours a day consumes 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 kWh daily, about 225 kWh over a thirty-day month, which at 15 cents per kilowatt-hour costs roughly 34 dollars. Contrast that with a 5 W phone charger left plugged in permanently: 5 W × 24 h × 30 days is 3.6 kWh, about 54 cents a month. The arithmetic explains why heating, cooling, water heating and tumble drying dominate household bills while standby loads, though worth trimming, are a rounding error by comparison.

The I²R form carries the single most important consequence in the whole of electrical engineering. Because loss scales with the square of current, halving the current in a cable cuts the heating loss to one quarter. For a fixed amount of power delivered, P = V·I means raising the voltage lets you lower the current proportionally. This is exactly why long-distance transmission lines run at 110,000 to 765,000 volts and step down through substations only near the point of use. It is also why undersized extension leads get warm, why a loose or corroded connection is a fire risk out of all proportion to its size (a high-resistance joint carrying full current dissipates real power in a tiny volume), and why aluminium house wiring earned a bad reputation when its connections loosened through thermal cycling.

sections.heading: Magnetism and electromagnetism
sections.body:
Magnetism and electricity are not two subjects but two aspects of one interaction, a unification worked out over the nineteenth century and completed by James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s. A permanent magnet has a north and a south pole; like poles repel, unlike poles attract. The decisive difference from electric charge is that magnetic poles have never been found in isolation. Cut a bar magnet in half and you do not get a north piece and a south piece; you get two complete magnets. Cut again and again, down to the individual atom, and each fragment still has both poles, because magnetism at root comes from the circulating motion and intrinsic spin of electrons, and a loop of current inevitably has two ends.

A magnet fills the space around it with a magnetic field, conventionally drawn as lines running out of the north pole, round through space, and into the south, closing on themselves inside the magnet. The closer the lines, the stronger the field. Field strength is measured in tesla: the Earth's field is a feeble 25 to 65 microtesla, a fridge magnet about 5 millitesla, a strong neodymium magnet up to about 1.4 tesla at its surface, and a clinical MRI scanner 1.5 to 3 tesla. The Earth behaves as though a bar magnet sat in its core, which is why a compass needle settles roughly north to south, though the magnetic poles wander and sit some distance from the geographic ones, an offset called magnetic declination that navigators must correct for.

The pivotal experiment came in 1820, when Hans Christian Ørsted noticed a compass needle twitch as he switched a nearby circuit, showing that an electric current creates a magnetic field. A straight current-carrying wire is encircled by field lines whose direction follows the right-hand grip rule: point the right thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers show the field direction. Wind that wire into a coil, or solenoid, and the individual loops reinforce one another to give a field like a bar magnet's. Slide an iron core inside and the iron's own atomic magnets align with the applied field and multiply it by a factor of hundreds or thousands. The result is an electromagnet: a magnet you can switch on and off, reverse by reversing the current, and strengthen by adding turns or current. Scrapyard cranes, relays, doorbells, loudspeakers, hard-drive actuators and MRI machines all depend on it.

The converse effect, found by Michael Faraday in 1831, is electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage in that coil. The word changing is essential. A magnet held still inside a coil produces nothing; move it, and current flows, faster movement giving more voltage. Faraday's law states that the induced electromotive force equals the rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit, and Lenz's law adds that the induced current always opposes the change producing it, which is simply conservation of energy in disguise and is why moving a magnet near a coil feels resistant. Nearly all the world's electricity is generated by this one principle.

sections.heading: Motors, generators, and electrical safety
sections.body:
Two machines exploit the link between electricity and magnetism, and they are essentially the same device run in opposite directions. An electric motor converts electrical energy into rotation. A current-carrying conductor sitting in a magnetic field experiences a sideways force, the motor effect, directed by Fleming's left-hand rule and of magnitude F = BIL for a wire of length L carrying current I across a field B. Wind the conductor into a coil on a shaft and that force becomes a torque. The complication is that after half a revolution the torque would reverse and stall the coil, so the current must be flipped at the right instant. A brushed DC motor does this mechanically with a split-ring commutator, which is why such motors wear at the brushes; brushless and induction motors let electronics or the alternating supply do it, which is why they now dominate.

A generator reverses the process by induction. Spin a coil inside a magnetic field, or magnets past fixed coils, and the changing flux induces a voltage. Because the flux changes sinusoidally as the coil turns, the natural output is alternating current. Whatever the prime mover — falling water, steam raised by coal, gas or nuclear fission, wind, or a diesel engine — the physics is identical: something turns a shaft. This also explains regenerative braking, where an electric vehicle's motor is driven backwards by the wheels and becomes a generator, returning energy to the battery instead of wasting it as brake-pad heat.

Electrical safety follows from the same equations. It is current through the body, not voltage alone, that injures. Roughly 1 mA is the threshold of sensation, 10 to 20 mA causes muscle contraction strong enough that a victim may be unable to let go of a conductor, and about 100 mA across the chest can throw the heart into ventricular fibrillation, which is fatal without prompt defibrillation. Since I = V/R, skin resistance decides the outcome. Dry, intact skin may offer 10,000 to 100,000 ohms, but wet or broken skin can fall to 1,000 ohms or less, so the same 230 V that gives a nasty jolt through dry hands can deliver a lethal 0.2 A through wet ones.

The protective devices each address a different failure. A fuse or circuit breaker interrupts excessive current before the wiring overheats and ignites, so it protects the building, not the person, and must never be replaced by a higher rating or bridged with foil. The earth conductor gives fault current a low-resistance path back to source, which both blows the fuse and holds exposed metalwork near ground potential. A residual-current device, sold as a GFCI in North America, compares the current flowing out with the current returning and trips within tens of milliseconds if as little as 30 mA goes missing, which is the only device that reliably protects a person. Treat every conductor as live until proven dead with a tester verified on a known live source, never assume a downed power line is dead, and leave mains and high-voltage work to licensed people.

sections.heading: Coulomb's Law and the Electric Field: Force at a Distance
sections.body:
Charles-Augustin de Coulomb established in 1785, using a torsion balance of his own design delicate enough to resolve forces of a few millionths of a newton, exactly how the force between two point charges depends on their size and separation: F = k·q₁q₂/r², where k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² is the Coulomb constant and r is the distance between them. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract, and the force falls with the square of distance, so doubling the separation cuts the force to a quarter rather than a half. Tripling it cuts the force to a ninth. The inverse-square form is shared with Newton's law of gravity and is no accident: both describe an influence spreading out over the surface of an expanding sphere, whose area grows as r².

It is often more useful to describe the influence a charge projects into the space around it without reference to whatever other charge might later arrive. Physicists therefore define the electric field E at a point as the force per unit charge that a small positive test charge placed there would feel: E = F/q, measured in newtons per coulomb or equivalently volts per metre. For a single point charge Q this evaluates to E = kQ/r². Field lines, an invention of Michael Faraday's, make the field visible on paper. They point the way a positive test charge would be pushed, radiate outward from positive charges and converge into negative ones, never cross, and are drawn more densely where the field is stronger. Between two large parallel plates the lines run straight and evenly spaced, giving a uniform field of magnitude E = V/d, which is the arrangement used inside capacitors and in the deflection plates of older oscilloscopes.

A worked example shows what the enormous constant k is compensating for. Two charges of one microcoulomb each, which is 10⁻⁶ C, separated by one metre, exert F = (8.99 × 10⁹)(10⁻⁶)(10⁻⁶)/1² ≈ 8.99 × 10⁻³ N, about nine millinewtons, roughly the weight of a small paperclip. A microcoulomb is already a large static charge in practice; a vigorously rubbed balloon typically carries far less. It takes a very large k to make such tiny quantities of charge produce a force you can feel at all.

That smallness is why measuring the charge on a single electron took until 1909, when Robert Millikan sprayed a fine mist of oil into the space between two charged horizontal plates and watched individual droplets through a microscope. By adjusting the plate voltage until a droplet hung motionless, he balanced the electric force qE exactly against the droplet's weight mg, and from the mass deduced by its unpowered fall rate he could compute the charge. The charges he found were always whole-number multiples of a single smallest value, e ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, demonstrating that charge is quantised. The result earned him the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics, and modern measurements place e at 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, a value now fixed exactly by definition of the ampere.

sections.heading: Capacitors: Storing Electric Charge — and Real Danger
sections.body:
A capacitor is a component built to store electric charge and the energy that comes with it. In its simplest form it is two conducting plates separated by a thin insulating layer called the dielectric. Connect it to a source and electrons pile onto one plate while an equal number are pulled off the other, leaving equal and opposite charge and an electric field in the gap. No charge crosses the dielectric; the current that appears to flow through a capacitor is really charge accumulating on one side and departing from the other.

The defining property is capacitance, C = Q/V, the charge stored per volt applied, measured in farads. The farad is so large that practical parts are rated in microfarads, millionths of a farad, or picofarads, million-millionths. Capacitance grows with plate area and with the dielectric constant of the insulator, and shrinks as the gap widens: C = εA/d. That is why electrolytic capacitors reach large values by growing a dielectric only nanometres thick on etched, convoluted aluminium foil, and why they are polarised: reversing the voltage destroys that oxide layer, often violently.

The stored energy is U = ½CV², growing with the square of the applied voltage exactly as a stretched spring's energy grows with the square of its extension. The parallel is not a coincidence: both come from integrating a linearly increasing quantity against a linearly increasing opposing one, and the ½ falls out of the integration. Doubling the working voltage quadruples the stored energy, which is why voltage rating, not capacitance, governs how dangerous a capacitor is.

A disposable camera's flash circuit charges a modest 150 μF capacitor to around 300 V; the stored energy is U = ½(150 × 10⁻⁶)(300)² = 6.75 J. That is a small number beside a car battery's reserves, but it is delivered in well under a millisecond, and the resulting peak power exceeds ten kilowatts. Through skin contact it gives a violent shock, and the startle response has caused injuries from falls. Anyone opening such electronics should discharge the capacitor deliberately through a resistor of a few kilohms rather than shorting it with a screwdriver, which welds tips and sprays metal. The same principle scales up in a defibrillator, which stores 100 to 360 J to shock the heart, and in microwave ovens, whose high-voltage capacitors hold a reliably lethal charge.

The key safety point is that a capacitor stays charged after the supply is removed. A resistive circuit is dead the instant the battery is disconnected; a capacitor is not, and a good dielectric may hold charge for minutes, hours or days. Large capacitors in power supplies and inverters carry bleeder resistors to drain them, but a failed bleeder is invisible from outside. Treat any capacitor above about 50 V as charged until you have measured it with a meter and confirmed otherwise, and be aware of dielectric absorption, in which a briefly shorted capacitor recovers a fraction of its voltage over the following minutes as charge trapped in the dielectric relaxes back out.

sections.heading: AC, DC, and the War of the Currents
sections.body:
Electricity comes in two fundamentally different forms. Direct current, or DC, flows steadily in one direction, which is what a battery, solar panel or DC power supply produces. Alternating current, or AC, reverses direction periodically, following a sine wave at 50 Hz across most of Europe, Asia and Africa and 60 Hz across the Americas. One consequence of the sine shape is that the quoted mains voltage is not the peak but the root-mean-square value, the equivalent steady voltage that would deliver the same heating power. A 230 V RMS supply actually peaks at 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V, the figure insulation must survive.

The reason nearly all long-distance transmission is AC comes down to one device: the transformer. Two coils wound on a shared iron core exchange energy through a changing magnetic field, and the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, so 1,000 turns feeding 100 turns steps 10,000 V down to 1,000 V while stepping current up by the same factor. Transformers need no moving parts and reach efficiencies above 99 per cent, but they depend absolutely on the field changing: steady DC produces no changing flux and therefore no output.

Why the ability to change voltage matters comes from the loss formula P_loss = I²R, which depends on the square of the current, not on the power being delivered. Since P = VI, delivering fixed power at higher voltage requires proportionally less current. Consider sending 100,000 W down a line of just 1 Ω resistance. At a household-scale 240 V the current would be I = P/V ≈ 417 A and the loss I²R ≈ 173,900 W, far more than the power being delivered, so the voltage would simply collapse before the load received anything useful. Step the transmission voltage up to 100,000 V and the same 100,000 W needs only 1 A, dropping the loss to a negligible 1 W. That is why grids transmit at hundreds of kilovolts and step down through substations near the point of use.

This is why AC won a genuine commercial battle in the 1880s and 1890s, remembered as the War of the Currents. Thomas Edison had built his business on low-voltage DC distribution, which worked but required a generating station roughly every mile because the losses forbade anything further. George Westinghouse, backed by Nikola Tesla's polyphase AC induction motor and transformer patents, offered a system that could send power tens of miles. The dispute grew ugly, but the engineering was decisive: the Adams Power Station at Niagara Falls, built to a Westinghouse and Tesla AC design and completed in 1895, transmitted hydroelectric power more than twenty miles to Buffalo, a feat DC systems of the era simply could not match.

The honest postscript is that DC has returned at the top end. Modern high-voltage direct-current links use power electronics rather than transformers to change voltage, and they beat AC over very long distances, in undersea cables where AC losses are prohibitive, and when joining unsynchronised grids. Electronics inside almost every device also run on DC, converted from the mains at the point of use.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
A basic circuits kit is inexpensive, widely stocked by electronics and hobby suppliers, and everything in it is reusable indefinitely. What matters is understanding what each item is for, because two of them are commonly bought in the wrong form.

The solderless breadboard is the most useful item and the most misunderstood. Beneath its surface sit rows of sprung clips: the long rails down each edge are continuous power buses, while the short rows in the central field join five holes and stop dead at the middle channel, sized so an integrated circuit can straddle it with each leg in its own row. Knowing that pattern is the difference between a circuit that works first time and an hour of confusion. Breadboards suit low voltage and modest current only, never mains.

The multimeter turns theory into measurement. Any inexpensive model with voltage, current and resistance ranges is adequate, but cheap meters share a limitation: the current ranges sit behind an internal fuse that blows if the meter is connected across a voltage source while still in current mode, so buy a spare fuse. Auto-ranging saves time, manual ranging teaches more, and a continuity beeper is worth having because tracing a break by ear beats watching a display.

A battery is chosen deliberately over a mains adaptor. A 9 V battery has an internal resistance of a few ohms, so even a dead short is self-limiting and cannot start a fire, which forgives the wiring mistakes every beginner makes. A resistor assortment matters because the exercises need specific values, and a kit spanning a few ohms to several megohms is cheaper than buying them one at a time. Learn the colour bands, or verify each value with the meter before trusting it.

The optional parts extend what you can observe. An LED demonstrates polarity, conducting only one way round, with a roughly fixed forward drop from 1.8 V for red to 3.2 V for blue. A small electrolytic capacitor lets you watch charging unfold: pair 100 μF with 100 kΩ and the time constant τ = RC is 10 seconds, slow enough to follow on a meter as the voltage climbs to 63 per cent of the supply in one time constant and is effectively full after five.
ingredients: A solderless breadboard (a plastic board with a grid of spring clips for building circuits without soldering)
A digital multimeter (any $15-30 model with voltage, current, and resistance/continuity settings)
A battery holder with fresh AA batteries, or a single 9V battery with a snap connector
An assortment pack of resistors covering a range of values (commonly sold as a 'resistor kit' with values from a few ohms to several megaohms)
A handful of jumper wires or breadboard wire, plus a couple of alligator-clip test leads
One or two small LEDs (useful bonus for observing polarity and voltage drop, though not required for the core exercise)
Optional: a small electrolytic capacitor (10-100 μF) if you want to extend the exercise to charge/discharge behavior

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build a Circuit and Verify Ohm's Law Yourself
sections.body:
Measuring a circuit you built yourself is what converts V = I·R from a memorised formula into something you believe. Two points of technique underlie the whole exercise. A voltmeter goes across a component, in parallel with it, because voltage is a difference between two points; its very high internal resistance, often 10 megohms, means it draws almost no current and barely disturbs what it measures. An ammeter goes in series, with the circuit physically broken and the meter inserted into the gap, because the current must pass through it; its internal resistance is very low for the mirror-image reason. Connecting an ammeter across a battery is close to a deliberate short circuit, and is the commonest way a first multimeter is destroyed.

Expect small discrepancies and understand them rather than dismissing them. Carbon-film resistors are typically ±5 per cent, so a nominal 470 Ω part may legitimately measure 447 to 494 Ω, and a battery's own internal resistance pulls its terminal voltage below its open-circuit value by exactly that resistance times the current. The parallel result is the one that defeats intuition: adding a resistor lowers total resistance and raises total current, which makes sense once you picture resistors as pathways rather than obstacles. Keep strictly to 9 V or less.
steps: Set your multimeter to measure resistance (Ω) and directly test one resistor from your kit — confirm its value against the color-code printed on it (or its labeled value if pre-marked) before building anything.
On the breadboard, connect the battery's positive terminal through the resistor to the negative terminal, forming a simple closed loop — this is your basic series circuit.
Switch the multimeter to DC voltage mode and measure the voltage across the battery terminals directly (record it — a fresh 9V battery often reads slightly above 9V).

Without disconnecting anything, switch the multimeter to DC current mode, break the circuit at one point, and insert the meter in series (current must flow THROUGH the meter, unlike voltage which is measured ACROSS a component) to read the circuit current in milliamps.

Calculate resistance from your own readings: R = V/I, and compare it to the resistor's labeled value — they should match closely (small differences come from the battery's own tiny internal resistance and the resistor's manufacturing tolerance, often ±5%).
Now add a second resistor in SERIES (end to end, in the same loop) and remeasure total current; verify that total resistance R_total = R₁ + R₂ by recomputing R = V/I_new.

Rebuild with the two resistors in PARALLEL instead (both connected across the same two points, giving current two separate paths) and remeasure; verify that 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ — you should measure a LOWER total resistance and HIGHER total current than either single resistor alone, which surprises most people the first time they see it.

Safety note: keep this experiment to low-voltage battery power only (9V or less) — never attempt to probe household mains wiring or outlets with a multimeter unless you are a trained, licensed electrician, since household current is genuinely lethal.

guides.title: Heat & Thermodynamics
guides.summary: Temperature versus heat, the three modes of heat transfer, specific heat and phase changes with real calculations, thermal expansion, the gas laws, and the four laws of thermodynamics that govern engines, refrigerators, and why perpetual motion is impossible.

sections.heading: Temperature vs heat: two different things
sections.body:
Everyday speech uses heat and temperature as though they mean the same thing, but physics draws a sharp line between them, and almost every confusion about thermal behaviour traces back to blurring it.

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance, which is to say how vigorously its molecules jiggle, vibrate or fly about on average. It is an intensive property: it does not depend on how much of the substance you have. Cut a hot bar in half and each half is still at the same temperature. Heat, written Q, is different in kind. It is energy in transit between objects because of a temperature difference, measured in joules like any other energy, and it flows spontaneously from hotter to colder and never the other way without work being done. Once heat has arrived somewhere it stops being heat and becomes part of that object's internal energy, which is why it is strictly wrong to say an object contains a certain amount of heat.

A lit match makes the distinction vivid. Its flame reaches roughly 800 °C, a far higher temperature than a bath at 40 °C, but the flame contains only a few milligrams of hot gas, so its total thermal energy is tiny. Drop the match into a full bathtub and the water temperature rises by an amount too small to measure, because the bath holds perhaps 150 kilograms of water whose combined internal energy dwarfs the match's. Temperature tells you how hot, quantity of matter tells you how much, and only the two together tell you how much energy is involved.

Three scales are in daily use. Celsius fixes 0 at water's freezing point and 100 at its boiling point under standard sea-level pressure. Fahrenheit, still standard in the United States, converts by °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32 and back by °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9. The two coincide at −40, a useful check when you doubt an arithmetic slip. Kelvin is the SI absolute scale, using the same degree size as Celsius but starting at absolute zero, so K = °C + 273.15. Absolute zero is 0 K, −273.15 °C or −459.67 °F.

Kelvin matters far more than a mere convenience. Every gas law, every efficiency calculation and every radiation formula requires absolute temperature, because those relationships are proportional to the total particle energy rather than to an arbitrary zero point. Halving 200 K genuinely halves the average particle energy, whereas halving 20 °C is meaningless. Absolute zero is the state of minimum possible particle motion, not total stillness, since quantum mechanics leaves a residual zero-point motion. It can be approached ever more closely, and laboratories have reached below a billionth of a kelvin, but it can never be reached, because each cooling step removes only a fraction of what remains.

sections.heading: The three modes of heat transfer
sections.body:
Heat moves from hot to cold by three distinct mechanisms, and almost every real situation involves at least two of them at once. Recognising which one dominates tells you what to change when something is too hot or too cold.

Conduction is transfer through direct contact, as fast-vibrating particles jostle their slower neighbours without the material itself moving. It dominates in solids, above all in metals, where free electrons carry energy alongside lattice vibrations. The rate follows Fourier's law: proportional to thermal conductivity, to cross-sectional area and to the temperature difference, and inversely proportional to thickness. The spread of conductivities is enormous. Copper conducts at about 400 watts per metre per kelvin, stainless steel about 16, glass around 1, wood roughly 0.15, and still air only 0.024. That last figure is the whole basis of insulation: fibreglass, foam, down and wool do not insulate because of what they are made of but because they trap air in pockets too small to circulate. It also explains why a metal handrail at 15 °C feels bitterly cold while wood at the same temperature does not; the metal drains heat from your skin hundreds of times faster, and your nerves report rate of heat loss, not temperature.

Convection is transfer by the bulk movement of a fluid. Heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises while cooler denser fluid sinks to replace it, setting up a circulating convection current. A domestic radiator warms a room this way rather than by radiation despite its name, which is why blocking one with a sofa wastes it. The same process drives thunderstorm updraughts, ocean currents and the convection cells inside the Sun. Forcing the flow with a fan or pump multiplies the rate several-fold, which is why a fan cools you on a still day and why wind chill is real: moving air strips away the thin warm boundary layer that otherwise clings to your skin.

Radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves, mostly infrared at everyday temperatures, and needs no medium at all. It crosses the vacuum of space, which is how the Sun's energy reaches Earth. Every object radiates according to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, in proportion to the fourth power of its absolute temperature, so doubling the temperature in kelvin multiplies the emitted power sixteen-fold. Dark matte surfaces both absorb and emit efficiently while shiny surfaces do neither, which is why emergency blankets are metallised and why light clothing is cooler. A vacuum flask defeats all three modes at once: an evacuated gap blocks conduction and convection, and silvered walls reflect radiation back where it came from.

In practice the modes always combine, and it pays to account for them separately. A mug of coffee loses heat by conduction into the table it stands on, by convection into the air rising off its surface, by radiation to the cooler walls, and by evaporation, a fourth route that carries away latent heat rather than transferring heat directly. A lid attacks evaporation and convection together and is worth more than any amount of insulation elsewhere.

sections.heading: Specific heat capacity and calorimetry
sections.body:
Different substances need very different amounts of energy to warm up by the same number of degrees. The property that captures this is specific heat capacity, written c, defined as the energy required to raise one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius, which is identical to one kelvin since the two scales use the same degree size. The working formula is Q = m·c·ΔT, where Q is the heat energy in joules, m the mass in kilograms, c the specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram per degree, and ΔT the temperature change.

Water is a striking outlier at 4,186 J/(kg·°C), several times higher than almost any common solid. The reason lies in hydrogen bonding: a large share of any energy added goes into stretching and breaking the weak bonds between molecules rather than into faster motion, so the temperature climbs reluctantly. Iron sits near 450, aluminium near 900, glass near 840, and dry air about 1,005 J/(kg·°C). Water's stubbornness has enormous practical reach. It moderates coastal climates, so an island rarely swings as far between summer and winter as a continental interior at the same latitude. It makes water the default coolant in engines, power stations and central heating. It is why a swimming pool stays cool while the paving beside it scorches, and why a hot-water bottle stays useful for hours whereas a hot brick of the same mass gives up its warmth quickly.

A worked example fixes the method. To heat 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C the temperature change is 80 °C, so Q = 2 × 4,186 × 80 = 669,760 J, close to 670 kJ. A 2,000 W kettle delivers 2,000 joules every second, so the theoretical minimum boiling time is 669,760 ÷ 2,000 ≈ 335 seconds, about five and a half minutes. Real kettles take longer because heat leaks through the walls and the element itself must warm up first, and because the quoted power is drawn at nominal mains voltage, which sags under load.

The same relationship underpins calorimetry, the technique of measuring thermal properties by tracking temperature alone. Its logic is conservation of energy applied to an insulated container: whatever heat a hot object gives up must equal the heat the surrounding cooler material takes in, so m₁c₁(T₁ − T_f) = m₂c₂(T_f − T₂). With every quantity known but one, that single equation yields the unknown. The main sources of error are honest and identifiable. Heat leaks out of the container, so real containers are insulated and their own heat capacity, called the water equivalent, is either measured or made negligible. Heat is lost during transfer of a hot sample, which biases the answer low. Stirring is needed for a true equilibrium reading but adds a little mechanical energy of its own. Good calorimetry is mostly a matter of making each of these effects smaller than the precision you actually need.

sections.heading: Phase changes and latent heat
sections.body:
When a substance changes state between solid, liquid and gas, something counter-intuitive happens: the temperature stops rising even though energy keeps pouring in. Heat a pan of ice-water and a thermometer sits stubbornly at 0 °C until the last ice has gone. The energy is not lost. It is being spent breaking the bonds that hold molecules in their ordered arrangement rather than making them move faster, and because temperature measures only average kinetic energy, the thermometer registers nothing. Energy stored this way is called latent heat, from the Latin for hidden, and it is released again in full when the change runs backwards.

The formula is simply Q = m·L, with Q in joules, m the mass in kilograms and L the specific latent heat in joules per kilogram. There are two values for each substance: the latent heat of fusion covers melting and freezing, and the latent heat of vaporisation covers boiling and condensing. For water, fusion takes 334,000 J/kg and vaporisation takes 2,260,000 J/kg. Vaporisation demands about 6.8 times more because melting only loosens molecules enough to slide past one another, whereas boiling must separate them completely against the full strength of their attraction.

A three-stage calculation shows the scale. Converting 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into steam at 100 °C requires melting the ice, 1 × 334,000 = 334,000 J; warming the resulting water from 0 to 100 °C, 1 × 4,186 × 100 = 418,600 J; and finally vaporising it, 1 × 2,260,000 = 2,260,000 J. The total is about 3,012,600 J, close to 3 MJ, and three quarters of it goes into the final boiling step alone. That is why a pan boils dry so slowly compared with how quickly it reached the boil, and why leaving a hob on under an empty pan is a sustained fire risk.

Three practical consequences follow directly. Sweating cools you because evaporating water draws its enormous latent heat from your skin; roughly a litre of sweat removes over two megajoules, which is why evaporative cooling is the body's most powerful defence against overheating. Steam burns are far more severe than boiling-water burns at the identical 100 °C, because condensing steam dumps 2.26 MJ per kilogram into the skin before it even begins to cool, which is why kettle spouts, pressure cookers and radiator caps deserve real respect. And ice is an efficient coolant precisely because melting absorbs 334 kJ/kg while the meltwater stays at 0 °C, so a drink holds steady until the last cube has gone and only then begins to warm.

Two related effects are worth knowing. Sublimation takes a solid straight to gas with no liquid stage: dry ice does this at −78.5 °C, ice cubes slowly shrink in a frost-free freezer for the same reason, and the process is the basis of freeze-drying. Water can also be supercooled several degrees below 0 °C while still liquid if it is pure and undisturbed; the instant something nucleates it, it freezes almost explosively and the latent heat released warms the slush straight back up to 0 °C.

sections.heading: Thermal expansion
sections.body:
Nearly every material grows when heated and shrinks when cooled. The mechanism is subtler than particles needing more room. The energy curve binding two neighbouring atoms is asymmetric: it rises steeply if they are pushed together and gently if they are pulled apart, so as vibration grows more violent the average separation drifts outward. That asymmetry, not the vibration alone, produces expansion.

For a rod or beam the change in length is ΔL = α·L₀·ΔT, where L₀ is the original length, ΔT the temperature change and α the coefficient of linear expansion, in units of one over degrees. Typical values are 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C for steel, 23 × 10⁻⁶ for aluminium, 9 × 10⁻⁶ for ordinary glass, 3.3 × 10⁻⁶ for borosilicate laboratory glass and about 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ for the nickel-iron alloy Invar, which was developed because it barely moves. Area expansion runs at roughly 2α and volume expansion at roughly 3α, which is why a heated metal plate's hole grows rather than shrinking, a result that surprises most people: the hole expands exactly as though it were filled with the same metal.

A 100 m steel bridge span warmed by 40 °C lengthens by ΔL = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 40 = 0.048 m, that is 4.8 centimetres. Restrained rather than free, that same expansion generates thermal stress of order α·E·ΔT, which for steel with a Young's modulus near 200 GPa is about 96 MPa, a substantial fraction of its yield strength. This is why bridges carry finger-plate expansion joints, why railway track is either gapped or laid pre-stressed as continuous welded rail, and why concrete pavements are cast in slabs with deliberate joints. Ignore it and rails buckle sideways in a heatwave, which railways treat as a derailment risk.

Everyday applications follow the same arithmetic. Running hot water over a stuck metal jar lid works because the metal's α exceeds the glass's, so the lid grows faster than the neck it grips. Liquid-in-glass thermometers work because mercury or dyed alcohol expands far more than the glass around it, amplified by the narrow bore. A bimetallic strip bonds two metals of different α so that heating forces it to curve toward the slower-expanding side, and that curvature is the switch inside mechanical thermostats, older thermal fuses and car indicator flashers. Pouring boiling water into thick ordinary glass cracks it because the inner surface expands before the outer has warmed, and the resulting stress exceeds glass's tiny tensile strength; borosilicate resists it because its α is a third as large.

Water is the famous exception. Between 0 °C and 4 °C it contracts as it warms and expands as it cools, reaching maximum density at about 4 °C, because the open hydrogen-bonded structure of ice persists partially in cold water. Ice is therefore about 9 per cent less dense than liquid water and floats. Lakes freeze from the top down, insulating the water beneath so fish survive the winter, and pipes burst when water freezes inside them.

sections.heading: The gas laws
sections.body:
Gases respond far more dramatically than solids or liquids to changes in pressure, volume and temperature, because their molecules are far apart and interact only in brief collisions. Three simple laws describe the behaviour, and every one of them requires absolute temperature in kelvin. Using Celsius produces nonsense, because the relationships are proportionalities and Celsius has an arbitrary zero.

Boyle's Law applies at constant temperature: P·V is constant, so pressure and volume are inversely related. Halve the volume and the pressure doubles, because the same number of molecules strike a smaller wall area more often. Charles's Law applies at constant pressure: V/T is constant, so volume rises in proportion to absolute temperature. A balloon taken outdoors on a cold day visibly shrinks. Gay-Lussac's Law applies at constant volume: P/T is constant, so heating a sealed rigid container raises its pressure, which is exactly why aerosol cans carry a warning against fire and against leaving them in a hot car.

The three merge into the combined gas law, (P₁V₁)/T₁ = (P₂V₂)/T₂, which handles any change where the amount of gas stays fixed. The fuller statement is the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, with P in pascals, V in cubic metres, n the amount of substance in moles, T in kelvin and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), the universal gas constant. The word ideal is an honest caveat: the law assumes molecules occupy no volume and do not attract one another. Real gases follow it closely at ordinary pressures and temperatures well above their boiling points, and depart from it near condensation or at very high pressure, which is where the van der Waals equation and its successors take over.

A worked example that matters on the road: a car tyre is inflated to P₁ = 200 kPa at T₁ = 290 K, which is 17 °C. An hour of motorway driving heats the air to T₂ = 320 K, about 47 °C, at essentially constant volume since the tyre is stiff. The new pressure is P₂ = P₁ × T₂/T₁ = 200 × 320/290 ≈ 221 kPa, a rise of about 10 per cent. That is why manufacturers specify cold pressures and why bleeding a hot tyre down to the placard figure leaves it dangerously underinflated once cool.

The safety consequences are serious and worth stating plainly. Never heat a sealed container of gas or liquid. Pressure climbs in proportion to absolute temperature with no relief, and containers fail suddenly rather than gently, throwing fragments. Aerosol cans and sealed bottles thrown on a fire become genuine shrapnel hazards. Sealed food jars can burst in a microwave. A closed vehicle in summer sun can reach 60 °C or more, enough to vent a lighter or a butane canister. The same physics also works for you: a pressure cooker deliberately raises the boiling point to about 120 °C at 200 kPa gauge, cooking food substantially faster.

sections.heading: The laws of thermodynamics
sections.body:
Four laws govern all heat, work and energy, from a kettle to the long-term fate of the universe. They are numbered oddly because the zeroth was recognised as fundamental only after the others had been named.

The Zeroth Law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. That sounds trivial but it is what makes temperature a meaningful, transitive property and what licenses the use of a thermometer at all: the instrument comes into equilibrium with the object, and reading the instrument therefore tells you about the object.

The First Law is conservation of energy stated for thermal systems: ΔU = Q − W, where ΔU is the change in a system's internal energy, Q the heat added to it and W the work it does on its surroundings. Energy is never created or destroyed, only moved and converted. The practical consequence is that no machine can deliver more energy than it receives, which rules out perpetual motion of the first kind. It also explains why a bicycle pump warms up as you compress air: the work you do goes into the gas's internal energy.

The Second Law is the deep one. Heat flows spontaneously only from hot to cold, and the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Entropy is a measure of how many microscopic arrangements correspond to the same overall state, so the law is at bottom a statement about overwhelming probability rather than a force. Its most consequential corollary is that no heat engine can be perfectly efficient: some energy must always be rejected to a cold reservoir, and the ceiling is the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_cold/T_hot with temperatures in kelvin. It also rules out perpetual motion of the second kind, a machine that would extract work from a single reservoir, and it gives time a direction, since the microscopic laws themselves run equally well backwards.

The Third Law states that as temperature approaches absolute zero, the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero, and that absolute zero is unattainable in a finite number of steps. Each stage of cooling removes only a proportion of the remaining energy, so the target recedes.

Two machine families follow directly. A heat engine, whether a petrol engine, a steam turbine or a power station, draws heat from a hot source, converts part of it to work and dumps the remainder to a cold sink; the cold sink is not waste through poor design but a thermodynamic requirement. A refrigerator or heat pump runs the same cycle backwards, spending work to move heat from cold to hot against its natural direction. That is why the coils behind a fridge are warm, and why leaving the door open heats the kitchen: the appliance dumps everything it removes plus the compressor's own energy back into the same room. The Second Law is the ultimate reason energy costs money and why efficiency can always be improved but never completed.

sections.heading: Heat Engines, Refrigerators, and the Carnot Limit
sections.body:
A heat engine is any device that converts a flow of heat from a hot reservoir to a cold one into useful mechanical work: a petrol engine, a steam turbine, a jet, a coal or nuclear power station. Its efficiency is η = W/Q_h, the work extracted divided by the heat drawn from the hot source.
