Almost everything needed to observe nuclear physics directly is inexpensive, generic and entirely safe when used as intended. The one firm rule is never to open a sealed source such as a smoke detector, because the sealing is precisely what makes it harmless.

A detector is the item that turns this subject from something read into something seen. An entry-level Geiger-Müller counter registers natural background at roughly 20 to 60 counts per minute depending on altitude and local geology, and that steady, irregular ticking is itself the lesson: radiation is ambient, ordinary and already all around you before any sample is introduced. Everything else on the list — a banana, a container of potassium-chloride salt substitute, an old thoriated lantern mantle — exists to give the counter something modestly above background to respond to, so the difference between ambient and elevated becomes audible rather than theoretical.

The radon test kit is the one item with genuine practical stakes rather than pedagogical ones, because it measures a real hazard in your own building. The coins and graph paper serve an entirely different purpose, converting the abstract exponential of decay into a curve you generate by hand out of pure randomness.
ingredients: A consumer-grade Geiger counter (sold by hobby-electronics and scientific-instrument retailers, both in stores and online; entry-level battery-powered models are relatively inexpensive) — for measuring background radiation and testing everyday mildly-radioactive items

A home radon test kit (short-term charcoal-canister or long-term alpha-track type; sold at hardware stores, or through state/local health-department programs, sometimes at reduced cost or free) — the single most actionable real-world safety application in this whole guide

A banana, or a container of a 'lite'/low-sodium salt substitute (potassium chloride, from a grocery store) — both are mildly, harmlessly radioactive from natural potassium-40 and make a safe, easy Geiger-counter calibration source

Optional, only if already owned secondhand: an old camping-lantern mantle or a piece of vintage orange 'uranium glass'-style glazed dinnerware — some older mantles and glazes used thorium or uranium compounds and are mildly radioactive; this is not something to seek out or purchase new

The smoke detector already installed in your home — do not open or disassemble it; it's simply a real-world example of a safely engineered sealed radioactive source, discussed in the applications section
100 identical coins, dice, or a bag of dried beans marked on one side, plus a large flat tray or box lid — for the hands-on half-life simulation below
Graph paper, a pencil, and a calculator or spreadsheet app, for plotting your simulated decay curve against the true exponential formula

Optional, for visualizing actual particle tracks: a basic cloud-chamber kit (dry ice, isopropyl alcohol, a dark box, and a strong flashlight, sold as a science-education kit or assembled from a felt strip, a clear container, and dry ice from a grocery or party-supply store) — makes cosmic-ray and natural background radiation tracks visible as tiny fog trails
A library or bookstore copy of an introductory nuclear or modern-physics textbook, for the deeper math behind the equations above

sections.heading: Step-by-step: simulate radioactive decay yourself, and watch the exponential curve emerge
sections.body:
This classic demonstration reproduces a smooth exponential curve out of purely random individual events, which is the conceptual heart of radioactive decay. Each coin stands for one nucleus, and each toss is one time step in which every nucleus independently faces a fifty per cent chance of decaying. Nothing keeps track of which coins were tossed before, and no coin is ever due — exactly the memorylessness of real nuclei, which have no internal clock and no history.

The reason the aggregate comes out so orderly despite the randomness of every individual event is simply the number of trials. With a hundred coins you expect fifty heads with a typical spread of around five, a ten per cent scatter clearly visible as wobble in the plotted points. A real source contains something like ten to the eighteenth nuclei, where the equivalent fractional scatter is around one part in a billion, which is why a decay curve measured in a laboratory looks perfectly smooth.
steps: Gather 100 identical coins (or dice, or marked beans) and a flat tray. Each coin represents one radioactive atom; 'heads' (or a specific die face, or the marked side) represents 'this atom decayed this round.'
Dump all 100 coins onto the tray in a single layer, count how many landed heads-up, and remove those coins — they've 'decayed.' Record the number REMAINING (should be roughly 50).
Take the remaining coins, shake and dump them again, count heads, remove them, and record the new remaining count (roughly 25).
Repeat — shake, count heads, remove, record remaining — until fewer than 2–3 coins remain (typically 6–8 rounds starting from 100 coins).
Plot your recorded 'remaining atoms' values against round number on graph paper (round number on the x-axis, coins remaining on the y-axis).

On the same graph, overlay the theoretical prediction N(t) = 100 × (1/2)^t for t = 0, 1, 2, 3… (each round is, by construction, exactly one 'half-life,' since every coin has a 50% chance per round) and compare how closely your real, randomly-generated data tracks the smooth curve — most home trials land within a coin or two of the prediction at every step.

Optional extension with your Geiger counter: place it a fixed distance from a mildly radioactive item from the tools list (a banana, a KCl salt substitute container, or an old lantern mantle if you have one) and record counts-per-minute over five 1-minute intervals; then double the distance and repeat — you should see the count rate drop by roughly the inverse square of the distance, a separate but related real radiation measurement doable with nothing but a basic detector and a tape measure.

Optional second extension: test your home's radon level with a purchased test kit, following its instructions exactly (correct placement in the lowest lived-in level, the specified sealed-room/windows-closed period, and mailing to or reading per the kit's specified process); compare your result to the EPA action level of 4 pCi/L from the applications section, and contact a licensed radon-mitigation professional if you're at or above it.

guides.safetyNote: Covers real radiation-dose figures, radon gas, and medical isotopes; any personal radiation exposure concern (home radon, occupational exposure, medical imaging/treatment questions) should go to a licensed radon-mitigation professional or a physician/health physicist, not be resolved from this guide alone.
